The 3 witnesses are Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer, and Martin Harris. The 8 witnesses are Hyrum Smith, Joseph Smith Sr., Samuel H. Smith, Jacob Whitmer, John Whitmer, Hiram Page, Christian Whitmer, and Peter Whitmer Jr. Joseph Smith, not counted amongst the witnesses, is the first prophet. The first thing that jumps out of this list is all of the Smiths and Whitmers. These are all members of the same two families. Additionally, Oliver Cowdery was David Whitmer's brother-in-law and Hiram Page was brother-in-law to all five Whitmer witnesses and also brother-in-law to Oliver Cowdery. Thus it appears that only Martin Harris had no direct familial ties through either blood or marriage to the two intermingled founding families of the LDS Church. One of the evidences put forth in favor of the validity of the testimonies of these witnesses is that they never recanted. Even those who left the Church for a brief period or forever apparently clung to the validity of their testimonies. There is a known phenomenon (with several names) wherein a family strictly sticks to a unified, often fabricated or defensive narrative. The principle of strength in unity which underlies the phenomenon has been known since at least the 6th century BCE, as seen in Aesop's Fable "The Father, his Sons, and the bundle of sticks". Conspiracy of Silence: An unwritten pact among family members to keep a secret, hide a crime, or maintain a single version of events and refuse to break rank. Unified Front / Closed Ranks: A behavioral term for a family that presents a single, unbreakable story to outsiders to protect themselves or cover up internal dysfunction. Folie à Famille ("Madness of Many" / Shared Psychosis): A clinical or psychological concept where a shared delusion or fixed false belief is transmitted from one or more family members to the rest of the household, causing them all to stick firmly to the same reality-detached story. Omertà: Originally a Mafia code of silence, this term is colloquially used for any tight-knit group or family bound by an absolute refusal to betray secrets or change their story. Family Saga: In literature and storytelling, a narrative that follows a family over time as they preserve a specific legacy, myth, or version of their history. This is a powerful phenomenon and the fact of such unity does not necessarily depend upon nor indicate truth. Has anyone ever suggested that the Witnesses employed something like what these Omerta-like phenomenons describe and, whether yes or no, does the LDS Church have any official response to the suggestion.

title: Voltage based LED dimmer for simulating day/night cycle
author: Raff89
text: I live far enough north, that during winter months, my alarm clock alone has a hard time convincing me that the day should start already. I was thinking about simulating the sunrise in my bedroom. I want to use popular 12V LED strips and drive them preferably without flicker. The system needs to handle some wattage, ~50W of LED strips initially, but I might want to use it elsewhere so I want it easily scalable. The whole thing has to be digitally controlled (via microcontroller). After moderately extensive googling session, I wasn't able to find a good ready-made candidate, so I thought: "Fine I'll do it myself". I am a software guy and I like to dabble in other domains - but full disclosure - my experience in electronics is limited to connecting some boards together and soldering things together at most. From what I've read, current limiting is the best way to go, but limiting voltage is also an option. I devised a plan and decided to put it out there on the internet for people to (hopefully constructively) criticize. My plan is as follows. Hardware: A cheap impulse PSU DC/DC voltage step-down regulator Digital potentiometer Microcontroller LED strips Setup: Solder the digital pot in place of adjustment pot on the converter (matching the resistance with resistors in series or parallel as needed). Hook the d-pot to a microcontroller and fine tune the converter's output voltage curve to achieve relatively smooth brightness adjustment. The thing I am worried about the most, is if a voltage controlled LED brightness is really that hard to do, I know that the curves of voltage to light output are steep but should be rather repeatable as long as the cheap upstream components won't make voltage drift unexpectedly. I also want to tinker with the idea without dumping significant amount of money into it, thus the cobbled together approach. An so the questions are: Is voltage adjustment practical for dimming the LEDs? Is the digital potentiometer soldered in place of adjustment pot on a DC/DC converter a sound idea? I am also open to completely different approaches, if within parameters: cheap + flicker-free + scalable in terms of power.

title: Why does a 40 MHz crystal XRCGB40M000F1S1BR0 produce a stable 96 MHz xtal clock signal under normal mode instead of 40 MHz?
author: Caelum
text: I tried different tests to understand and wish you can help to clarify the reason: What's the plausible reason for which the crystal explained below produces 96 MHz instead of 40 MHz, is it a design issue or is the part dysfunctional? As you can see on the pictures below, my PCB is based on ESP32S3 with a crystal XRCGB40M000F1S1BR0 whose fundamental frequency is 40 MHz. The load capacitance required by its datasheet is 8 pF, so I added a 12 pF to each of the two crystal's terminals and assumed 2 pF of stray capacitance: i.e. load_cap = (C1xC2)/(C1+C2) + C_stray = 6 pF + C_stray = 8 pF. The 24 nH serves to filter out the coupled noise as recommended by the Espressif Technologies. The resulting xtal clock signal is measured at 96 Mhz using both: (1) oscilloscope on the xtal_p of the MCU, (2) and by measuring the xtal clock signal frequency exposed through GPIO (I used clockout1 and GPIO20 as output pin) using an external frequency counter. Both tests led to 96 MHz, which is x2.4 increase (96 = 2.4 x 40). Even the ROM loader message at the startup (i.e. "board name, date of last upload") requires 2.4 x 115200 = 276480 baud to be read through UART, which strengthens further that the system is being fed by 96 MHz instead of 40 MHz. The XRCGB40M000F1S1BR0 vendor said that they tested other identical parts they have and that they found acceptable result shown on the table below. A little list of candidate causes in my opinion, hopefully you can share yours: A: the part is dysfunctional or not the exact part. B: My design encouraged higher harmonics such as 120 MHz and 80 MHz which led in average to 96 MHz but the oscilloscope didn't show varying periods. C: My design such as the placement or over stitching may cause that although I don't think the parasitic inductance from the later would be significant to the internal inductance of the crystal. Tools used: the stm32F429-disc1 internal timer with the external trigger ETR with divider 4 as frequency counter. this setup was used on commercial board and led to accurate result such commercial ESP32-cam. The oscilloscope is Tektronics 454 150Mhz, with the 10.5pF probe P6106.

title: Single phase Dual converter circuit using two phase converters
author: Amit M
text: This is a circuit for a dual converter i.e a phase converter that operates in I, II, III and IV quadrants of voltage and current at the load. It consists of two phase converters connected to a common load. I had used BTW69-1200 SCRs from ST microelectronics for the simulation in LTspice. Circuit: Waveforms: Output Voltage and current quadrants The current direction of \$ I_{dc}\$ going down towards the return path shown in the circuit diagram is positive. Output voltage \$ V_{dc}\$ and current \$ I_{dc}\$ can be positive or negative. The table below summarizes their attributes in all quadrants. $$ \begin{array}{|c|r|l|} \hline \textbf{Quadrant} & \textbf{Vdc} & \textbf{Idc} \\ \hline \text{I} & \text{+ve} & \text{+ve} \\ \hline \text{II} & \text{+ve} & \text{-ve} \\ \hline \text{III} & \text{-ve} & \text{-ve} \\ \hline \text{IV} & \text{-ve} & \text{+ve} \\ \hline \end{array} $$ $$ \text{Table 1} $$ It seems that the load can can have load current ( \$ I_{dc}\$) and the output voltage (\$V_{dc}\$ as positive and negative values. The gate currents have to be supplied at appropriate intervals so that output voltage and currents in quadrants I, II, III or IV as shown in the table 1. Table 1 lists the quadrants in which \$V_{dc}\$ and \$ I_{dc}\$ are positive or negative. Both converters 1 and 2 cannot be on at the same time as that would cause inconsistent output voltage and current results. Therefore, I had supplied the gate currents for SCRs U5, U6, U7 or U8 at the end of 20 ms interval which U1, U2, U3 or U4 were on. This prevents both converts to be on at the same time. I was thinking of an automated way of triggering the SCRs with automated gate circuits so that both converters can't be on at the same time as they share the same load. I am also looking into circuits for generating the gate current pulse instead of using LTspice provided current sources. Here is a summary of the SCRs that are on or off in different quadrants in Table 2. $$ \begin{array}{|c|r|l|} \hline \textbf{Quadrant} & \textbf{U1} & \textbf{U2} & \textbf{U3}& \textbf{U4} & \textbf{U5} & \textbf{U6} & \textbf{U7} & \textbf{U8} \\ \hline \text{I} & \text{on} & \text{on} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} \\ \hline \text{II} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{on} & \text{on} & \text{off} & \text{off} \\ \hline \text{III}& \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{on} & \text{on} \\ \hline \text{IV} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{on} & \text{on} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} & \text{off} \\ \hline \end{array} $$ $$ \text{Table 2} $$ LTspice Asc file BTW69-1200 Datasheet specifications BTW69-1200 subcircuit configuration An alternative question about a dual converter is here: Single phase dual converter waveform This doesn't address triggering SCRs with gate currents and its circuit connections are different from mine.

title: Preventing GPIO pin damage between devices when contention is expected to occur
author: CMPXCHG8B
text: I am trying to hook up the 1PPS output from a u-blox ZED-F9T module to the GPIO inputs of an Intel Atom E3845 based SBC. The SBC is using a UM3204UE level shifter to convert between 3.3v (GPIO side) and 1.8v (SBC side), apparently with a 4.7k pull-up resistor on the SBC side. Unfortunately the board in question has firmware that defaults the SBC GPIO ports to outputs being driven low by default. I cannot change this until the operating system has initialized and I have a chance to instruct the hardware to toggle those pins into input mode instead. Predictably I would like to ensure that the ZED-F9T module is not damaged during system boot. What is the best way to protect both devices from a situation like this? I've read conflicting things online that a simple 1-1.8k resistor wired in-line between both devices might be enough, but also that it might be better to just use something like an opto-isolator instead (though given that this is a 1PPS output from a high precision timing device, I'd prefer to try and introduce as little latency into the chain as possible). Due to the cost of the ZED-F9T modules, I'm also wondering if it would be worth it to consider the situation where the SoC GPIO pins are accidentally driven high as well, which is making me think that some sort of one-way isolation circuit would be best to consider so that the 1PPS output is totally protected from the SoC driving the GPIO lines high or low. Edit for more details: This is for a personal project to build a replacement Stratum 1 NTP time server for some older hardware I had that recently died. The target SBC is a Boingfire BFN5 based board, which I was initially lead to believe could be set to boot up with the GPIOs in an input state but it's actually only high/low outputs instead (hence my original question- I'm not too thrilled about this, but that's just the way things worked out). The ZED-F9T was chosen because I could get it for a decent price from Europe versus the insane cost of buying a u-blox module of any kind from Digikey/Mouser in Canada. It's totally overkill, but this is also just a hobby for me at the time being. According to Boingfire, the UM3204UE is attached directly to the E3845 SoC and does not go through an I2C adapter of any kind (which I've verified myself). Those GPIOs are capable of triggering system-level interrupts once reconfigured by the OS, so no problems there. The plan was to build a custom LFS-based distro with some real time kernel patches and other tweaks to try and get the NTP accuracy down to sub-1uS to meet or beat the accuracy of an old LeoNTP unit I had that recently died.

title: Two parallel circuits connected by a wire
author: Bodhisattva
text: I am learning how an old rotary phone works. The circuit diagram is as follows: The 48 V is typical of a PBX, and the 1.6 \$\text{k}\Omega\$ resistor is the loop resistance of the PBX. The loop current is \$ \frac{48}{1600} = 30 \text{ mA}\$. As the rotary is pressed down and returns, the contact breaks and makes continuously that corresponds to the digits. The time for each pulse is \$100\text{ ms}\$ and inside each pulse the make time is \$62\text{ ms}\$ and the break time is \$38\text{ ms}\$. The PBX detects the change in loop current to read the pulses made by the rotary. The \$40 \text{ H}\$ inductor is the bell that rings when a call comes. My understanding is that when contact breaks, the circuit is in series. Due to the large inductance of the bell (i.e. large reactance), current roughly flows through the \$ 1.6 \text{ k}\Omega\$ resistor and then the \$ 330 \text{ }\Omega\$ resistor and then the capacitor. The time constant of the RC circuit is \$1.9\text{ ms}\$. Since the time constant is very small compared to the break time of the circuit, which is \$38\text{ ms}\$, the circuit will saturate to \$0\text{ A}\$ for most of the break time. When the contact makes again, the PBX circuit above and the rotary circuit below forms a parallel circuit and the current flows through the contact. The current from the PBX circuit to the contact is again \$ \frac{48}{1600} = 30 \text{ mA}\$. Since the capacitor is saturated initially, it has a voltage of 48 V. Then current flows through the \$ 330 \text{ }\Omega\$ resistor with a value of roughly \$ \frac{48}{330} = 145 \text{ mA}\$ (assuming all current flows through the resistor and not the inductor). Will the current drop to zero after a few time constants given by \$ 330 \times 10^{-6} = 0.33 \text{ ms}\$? I guess it will not, because the capacitor is continuously being charged by the PBX circuit. Note that the end of the capacitor is connected to the negative terminal of the PBX.

title: Samtec SEAMP or SEAFP Press-Fit Retention Issue — Would Reducing PCB Thickness Actually Help?
author: B J
text: We're currently working with a Samtec SEAMP 40×8 press-fit connector on a custom 4-layer FR-4 PCB, and we're experiencing poor mechanical retention. The connector can become detached from the PCB relatively easily. For the PCB design, we used the official footprint library provided directly on Samtec's website, without intentionally modifying the recommended press-fit hole or pad dimensions. Current PCB specifications: Nominal PCB thickness: 1.6 mm Stack-up thickness: approximately 1.584 mm (excluding outer coatings) Nominal PTH diameter: 0.46 mm PTH pad diameter: 0.79 mm Number of press-fit contacts: 320 Contact type: Eye-of-the-Needle PCB construction: 4-layer FR-4 Background and my personal thoughts According to Samtec's official documentation, the minimum PCB thickness for this press-fit termination is approximately 1.575 mm. The documentation also explains that the Eye-of-the-Needle compliant section does not necessarily need to be centered within the PCB, provided that the contact is seated to the specified depth. However, our PCB manufacturer has suggested using a thinner PCB instead of the current 1.6 mm design. Personally, I'm not entirely convinced that reducing the PCB thickness would improve the situation. I understand that proper seating of the connector housing standoffs against the PCB is an important requirement for correct press-fit assembly. However, my concern is that if the PCB becomes too thin, the effective engagement between the Eye-of-the-Needle compliant section and the plated through-hole might be reduced, even when the connector housing is fully seated. If this happens, I suspect that the reduced contact engagement could potentially weaken the mechanical retention force and possibly affect electrical contact reliability, including contact resistance or connection stability. Since Samtec explicitly specifies a minimum PCB thickness, I'm wondering whether reducing the thickness below the current design would actually be a reasonable solution. Of course, this is only my personal engineering hypothesis, and I may be overlooking other mechanical factors involved in press-fit retention. My questions Can reducing PCB thickness actually improve press-fit retention? Or could a thinner PCB reduce the effective engagement of the compliant section and potentially decrease retention force? How strongly does the axial position of the Eye-of-the-Needle compliant section within the PCB affect the actual retention force? I'm wondering whether our PCB manufacturer's recommendation to use a thinner board might be related to the position of the compliant section within the plated through-hole. Would positioning the compliant section closer to the center of the PCB thickness actually improve mechanical retention? Or is the specified insertion depth and the resulting contact pressure against the PTH wall more important than the relative position of the compliant section? I'm particularly interested in understanding whether there is a meaningful relationship between the axial position of the compliant section and the actual pull-out force. If the official Samtec footprint library was used and the nominal PCB thickness meets the manufacturer's requirements, what would be the most likely causes of poor retention?

What I need help with is understanding whether I have chosen the correct power supply that will fulfill all of these requirements and how I should connect each internal device to ground. title: How to measure 1 mA to 20 A AC accurately on a 220 V line in a compact module
author: Rajanand
text: I’m designing a compact home IoT smart switch that must measure the current of a 220 V / 50 Hz AC load from about 1 mA to 20 A (a dynamic range of roughly 20,000:1). I need good accuracy across the range, especially at the low end, so small loads like standby devices and LED drivers register. Requirements: AC mains 220 V, 50 Hz, load up to 20 A (inrush to ~40 A) Lowest useful current: 1 mA, but 5 mA would be acceptable if 1 mA is unrealistic Accuracy target: about ±1% above 100 mA, and as good as possible below that Output to an ESP32 (I²C, SPI or UART) Galvanic isolation of the sensing element preferred What I’ve considered: Shunt + metering IC: a 1 mΩ shunt gives only 1 µV at 1 mA, and the board sits at mains potential. One CT + metering IC: e.g. NJXS TAB06C 20A/10mA (2000:1, class 0.1, 3 kV/1 min). Its datasheet gives accuracy only at rated current into a 20 Ω burden, and the body is about 27.5 × 25.2 × 16 mm, so it is too large. Smaller CT: e.g. NJXS DL-CT03CL 20A/10mA (2000:1, class 0.2, 18 mm OD, 5 mm hole). Again, no low-current accuracy data. Two CTs on the same wire: a 0.5A/0.5mA CT (1000:1) for the low range plus a 20A/10mA CT for the high range, read on two channels of a dual-current-channel IC such as the BL0939 (listed 4000:1 dynamic range, 10 mA to 35 A with a 1 mΩ shunt) or the ADE7953, with firmware switching between channels. My concerns: CT magnetizing error at currents far below the rated current. The small CT would see the full 20 A and may saturate or overheat. Do I need input clamping, and is it safe to use at that current? Do I need burden resistor selection for each CT given the metering IC’s input range (my guess for * the BL0939 is a few ohms for the 20 A CT, but I haven’t verified the datasheet)? Heat in a sealed enclosure at 20 A. Questions: Is a two-CT, two-channel approach a sound way to cover 1 mA to 20 A, or is there a better architecture? What accuracy can I realistically expect from a ring-core CT at 1 mA to 5 mA primary, and how should I calibrate it? Are there compact CTs or sensors (≤ 20 mm) that are actually specified for low-mA accuracy at 220 V? Is the BL0939 suitable for this, or should I use a discrete front end with a 24-bit ADC? Thanks for any advice. I know this is mains voltage, so I’ll follow proper isolation and safety practices.

text: I am designing a high-speed SiPM (Onsemi C series 60035) readout circuit and I am encountering a severe, reproducible simulation error specifically with the TLV3603 macro-model in TINA-TI. I have successfully isolated the problem to the comparator stage. Here is the exact breakdown of my circuit: Stage 1: The TIA (OPA855) - WORKING PERFECTLY Power: +5V and -5V. Topology: Transimpedance. + pin grounded. Rf = 10kΩ, Cf = 3pF. Input includes a 53.8pF capacitor to simulate the SiPM. Input: -100µA current pulse. Result: TINA simulates this flawlessly. The output is a clean, negative-going pulse dropping from 0V to -1.0V, with the standard RC recovery tail. Stage 2: The Comparator (TLV3603) - SIMULATION FAILS Because the TLV3603 is a single-supply comparator (+5V and GND), I cannot feed it the negative TIA pulse directly. I am using standard AC-coupling (similar to your TLV3603 datasheet application circuits): AC Coupling: 100nF capacitor from the TIA output to IN+. DC Bias: 100kΩ resistor from IN+ to a 1.2V DC source (so IN+ rests at 1.2V and drops to 0.2V during the pulse). Threshold: IN- is tied to a 0.6V DC source. Hysteresis: LE/HYS is tied to Ground via a 150kΩ resistor. The Error: When I run a Transient analysis, the simulation fails entirely. title: Operation and control of a half bridge N MOSFET
author: Curious Cat
text: Hello all, I am new to PCB fabrication and design in general. I have some questions about the operation and control of a half bridge N MOSFET. What you see in the image is a control circuit which basically receives a control signal from INA and INB to control PIN diodes driven by a half bridge MOSFET for the first two PIN diodes, and a "buffer" for the third PIN diode. In short, I want to check if this explanation of how the circuit works is correct INA and INB receive complementary signals (to prevent both transistors from turning on at same time). When INA receives an active high (INB should receive an active low), OUTA of the level shifter/isolator pulls to 0 V. Relative to the driver's negative reference of -5 V, this 0 V represents a logic HIGH to the driver. Because IN_H receives a logic HIGH, the driver commands the high side (100 V) of the half bridge to turn on, while InL is LOW, so the low side channel is OFF. Using the charge previously stored in the bootstrap capacitor between pins BST and HS, the driver applies the floating bootstrap voltage across the gate and source. Pin DH (connected to gate of high N-FET) is driven up to approximately 110 V. The lowside N-FET source is tied to -5 V and the gate (DL) also sits at -5V due to it being clamped down to -5 V from the LOW signal at IN_L(?). The highside N-FET drain connects to 100 V, source connects to switching node Vmid and gate is at ~110 V. Resulting gate to source voltage is ~10 V, turning this transistor fully ON. With high side FET conducting and low side off, node Vmid is pulled up to 100 V. This 100 V will reverse bias the PIN diodes and they will appear as open circuit, not allowing signals to pass from RFin to RFout. When INB receives the HIGH, it will be the low side transistor that activates and Vmid pulls to -5 V, forward biasing the PIN diodes and allowing signals to pass.

ORIGEN interprets the glorified body as a new, spiritual, luminous, and ethereal body, rejecting the notion that it will consist of literal, dense, earthly flesh and bone. Heavily influenced by Saint Paul’s concept of the "spiritual body" (soma pneumatikon) in 1 Corinthians 15, Origen argued that our current heavy, corruptible flesh is a consequence of the Fall and must be radically transformed to inherit the celestial realm. Origen's perspective on the resurrection body hinges on several key theological frameworks: (i) Ethereal and Luminous Substance: Origen believed that the resurrected body is adapted to inhabit heaven, the substance of which was traditionally thought to be ether. He described the glorified bodies of the saints as becoming like those of angels—composed of a highly refined, "bright light" (augoeides phōs). (ii) Form (Eidos) vs. Material: To reconcile his spiritual view with the biblical promise of resurrection, Origen made a distinction between the temporary material of the body (which changes constantly like a river) and its underlying structural form or principle (eidos).

title: Daniel 9:26 - What were the ethnicities of the people who destroyed Jerusalem in 70AD?
author: Alan Nicholson
text: [Daniel 9:26] – “the people of the prince who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary.” In this verse we are told it is “the people of the prince” not the “the kingdom of the prince.” If “kingdom” was intended then the appropriate Hebrew word would be “mamlakah” H4467. “People” is translated from the Hebrew word “ʿam” H5971 which means "people," "nation," or “kin." It describes a collective group, tribe, or population, such as Am Yisrael (the People of Israel) in Modern Hebrew. Unlike another Hebrew word “goy“ H1471 which can be translated “nation” but generally refers to a foreign nation or ethnic group, “ʿam” emphasizes close family bonds, relatedness, and shared identity. Simply stated “ʿam” refers to ethnicity not citizenship. The apostle Paul was a citizen of Rome but he was ethnically a Jew. Consequently, to help in our understanding of the meaning of this verse we need to determine what were the ethnicities of the people who destroyed the city (Jerusalem) and the sanctuary (Temple) in 70AD. For instance: An army of 60,000 soldiers attacked Jerusalem Josephus tells us that, “the whole army, including the auxiliaries sent by the kings, as well horsemen and footmen, when all were united together, amounted to sixty thousand” (Josephus, Wars, Book 3, Chapter 4, Paragraph 2). Approximately 25,000 were Roman Legionaries Speaking of the Roman attack of Jerusalem, Tacitus details the specific legions and the peoples that primarily composed the attacking army: Titus Caesar… found in Judaea three legions, the 5th, the 10th, and the 15th… To these he added the 12th from Syria, and some men belonging to the 18th and 3rd, whom he had withdrawn from Alexandria. This force was accompanied… by a strong contingent of Arabs, who hated the Jews with the usual hatred of neighbors… (Tacitus The History New Ed edition Book 5.1 Editor: Moses Hadas). An average size Roman legion consisted of 5,000 legionaries. Tacitus implies there were four average size legions: 5th Macedonia, 10th Fretensis, 15th Appoinaris, and 12th Fulminata; plus two partial size legions: 18th and 3rd Gallica. Consequently there were about 25,000 legionaries plus 35,000 “auxiliaries” from the surrounding area. Tacitus says "This force (Roman Legions) was accompanied… by a strong contingent of Arabs." Before digging any deeper, it appears that over half of the attacking army was not Italian but Arab! Revised Question In the text, "the prince who is to come" is a reference to a future prince not the prince of 70AD. The action is by "the people (ethnic group who)... will destroy the city and sanctuary." Many seem to view this verse as we know "the prince who is to come" is from the Roman Empire therefore the people (ethnic group) that destroyed Jerusalem must be of Roman ethnicity. Prophecy predicts the future not the past. The destruction of Jerusalem in 70AD occurs first then the coming prince sometime later.

title: Did Descartes actually solve the tangent problem for his own Folium of Descartes?
author: HGF
text: I am currently studying the historical debate between Pierre de Fermat and René Descartes regarding the method of finding tangents in the 1630s. To challenge Fermat's "method of adequality" (which was perceived as cumbersome), Descartes famously constructed the curve $x^3 + y^3 = pxy$, now known as the Folium of Descartes, and challenged Fermat to find its tangent. 1. Fermat's Method (Adequality) Fermat's approach was remarkably elegant and algorithmic. By substituting a small increment $x \mapsto x+e$ and $y \mapsto y+ke$ (where $k$ is the tangent slope), he established an "adequality" ($\bumpeq$): $$ (x+e)^3 + (y+ke)^3 \bumpeq p(x+e)(y+ke) $$ By expanding, canceling the original equation $x^3+y^3=pxy$, dividing by $e$, and discarding the remaining terms containing $e$, he easily obtained: $$ 3x^2 + 3ky^2 = p(y+kx) \implies k = \frac{py - 3x^2}{3y^2 - px} $$ 2. Descartes's Method of Normals and His Dilemma Descartes, on the other hand, used his "method of normals" (the circle method). He would construct a circle with center $(v, 0)$ intersecting the curve, and set the condition that the intersection is a double root to represent tangency. However, for the Folium, substituting the circle's equation $y^2 = R^2 - (x-v)^2$ into the curve results in a massive algebraic nightmare. It leads to a 6th-degree polynomial in $x$: $$ x^6 = \left[ x^2 + (p-2v)x + (v^2-R^2) \right]^2 \cdot \left[ R^2 - (x-v)^2 \right] $$ To find the normal, Descartes would have to expand this completely and equate its coefficients with $(x-x_0)^2$ and a 4th-degree polynomial. This is an extremely tedious task to do by hand, highly prone to errors. 3. The Core Question: Did Descartes actually solve it? I am aware of Victor Katz's commentary (A History of Mathematics), which notes that Descartes criticized Fermat because he had independently discovered his own method and was proud of it. However, given the algebraic "disaster" of the 6th-degree polynomial, I am trying to trace the historical record: Did Descartes actually succeed in finding the tangent to the Folium of Descartes using his own circle method? Or did he fail the challenge he set for Fermat, leading him to avoid publishing the solution for this specific curve? Any references to Descartes's original correspondence or historical analyses on whether he actually completed the computation for this specific curve would be greatly appreciated. Thank you!

author: Al Berko
text: Hebrew is traditionally considered the Holy Tongue in which the world was created, yet its vocabulary for God and the divine realm seems to be derived almost entirely from the earthly, human world. "Panim / Yad": denote human body parts. "Amar / Diber / Yarad / Yashav": ordinary human actions, with no distinct verbs for divine interactions. no distinctive terms for the divine realm - שמים, מלאכים, אלוהים, עולם הבא, נבואה and more Etc. I considered several possible explanations that might align with rabbinic tradition, but each seems to raise difficulties: "People would not understand." Yet tradition holds that earlier generations were intellectual giants, capable of grasping profound theological concepts. "Words must always be grounded in human experience." Yet the verb bara, in the sense of "create," is used exclusively for God (although it appears in Joshua and Ezekiel with different meanings). "A distinct divine vocabulary was passed down orally." Yet we find no clear traces of such a vocabulary. Instead, God is referred to as HaShem or HaMakom. "It was a deliberate choice by the Torah, since 'the Torah speaks in the language of human beings' (Berakhot 31b)." However, this principle is generally invoked to explain specific textual features, such as repetitions, hyperbole, and common idioms, rather than the vocabulary of the entire Hebrew Bible. So why doesn't Hebrew have a distinct vocabulary for describing transcendent realities without relying so heavily on physical and human analogies? Why aren't there distinctive terms for שמים, מלאכים, אלוהים, עולם הבא, נבואה etc? I would also welcome references to any Hebrew terms used exclusively for God or the divine realm, and never for human or earthly things. This question is a "continuation" to many questions that deal with Biblical anthropomorphism (like The language of man & (mis)understanding G-d) - let alone the anthropomorphic language, why there's no divine vocabulary at all?

title: Why does Humanity and the animal kingdom depend on consuming living beings?
author: Al Berko
text: NB: This question is NOT not about post Noahide permission to animals and humans to consume other animals. One fundamental difference between plants and animals is how they obtain nourishment: Plants produce their own organic matter through photosynthesis, using sunlight, water, CO₂, and minerals (aka autotropy). Animals, including humans, MUST consume organic matter that consists of living cells (micro organisms - aka heterotropy): fresh fruits and vegetables consist of living plant cells (we don't consume cells that die naturally - decompose) meat and eggs consist of living cells we "kill" by cooking before consumption milk - living cells nuts and seeds are dormant living cells The Torah describes God providing vegetation as food for humans and animals (Genesis 1:29–30), and Sanhedrin 59b teaches that Adam was initially forbidden to eat meat. Yet even this original arrangement required living creatures to consume biological material from other living organisms, or, in other words, to kill living organisms. I find it difficult to understand why an omnipotent and benevolent Creator would choose such a system in the first place (before the human fall). God could easily have created animals, including intelligent and morally responsible humans, capable of sustaining themselves through photosynthesis or some other process using only inorganic substances and external energy. This would eliminate the biological necessity for one creature to consume another, along with much of the predation, competition, and suffering associated with obtaining food. In this question, I don't judge. Don't say whether it is good or bad, intelligent or not. I only focus on the reason why the world would function like this. I also understand that the fact that all plant and animal tissue consists of living cells was not known until the Renaissance. Do Jewish commentators or philosophers explain why God created animal life dependent on consuming other organisms, rather than making all living beings capable of obtaining nourishment directly from the non-living environment? What theological purpose does this dependence serve?

title: Why does Tanakh consistently portray angels as ordinary humans despite the danger of anthropomorphism?
author: Al Berko
text: The Torah strongly discourages attributing physical form to God. Deuteronomy 4:15–16 emphasizes that Israel saw no form at Sinai and warns against making images in the likeness of men or women. Yet Tanakh repeatedly describes God's heavenly messengers (מלאכים means messenger) as ordinary human beings, for example: Genesis 18:2–8: Three men (שלשה אנשים) visit Abraham, who offers them food, which they apparently eat. In Genesis 19:1, two of these visitors are identified as angels (מלאכים). Genesis 32:25–31: Jacob wrestles with a man (איש), subsequently declaring that he has seen God face to face. Hosea 12:5 identifies his opponent as an angel. Judges 13:6–22: Manoah's wife initially describes her visitor as a man of God (איש האלהים). After discovering that he was an angel, Manoah exclaims, "כי אלהים ראינו" — "For we have seen God/a divine being." This portrayal continues throughout rabbinic literature. Bereishit Rabbah 77:3 ("מִי נִתְמַלֵּא אָבָק הָאִישׁ שֶׁעִמּוֹ") describes the angel wrestling with Jacob as appearing in the guise of a herdsman; Midrash Tanchuma, Vayeshev 2 identifies the ordinary man who encounters Joseph (Genesis 37:15) as the angel Gabriel; and Moed Katan 28a describes the Angel of Death appearing to Rabbi Chiyya disguised as a poor man. Likewise, Bava Metzia 86b explains that the angels visiting Abraham appeared to eat and drink like ordinary guests. Thus, both biblical and rabbinic literature repeatedly reinforce the perception that angels can look and behave just like human beings. Maimonides maintains that angels are incorporeal (Mishneh Torah, Yesodei HaTorah 2:3–4) and explains their appearances as prophetic visions. Interestingly, Maimonides himself recognizes in Guide I:49 that corporeal descriptions of angels risk confusing their nature with that of God. Ramban (Genesis 18:1) instead describes angels appearing in perceptible forms or "garments." If so, the human form that the angels assume (as described in the Scripture) is a deliberate decision. I can easily imagine that angels would appear as something completely different from common forms, for example, suspended transparent spheres. My question is: Why does Scripture repeatedly choose human forms for God's heavenly representatives, rather than distinctly nonhuman appearances, such as fire or other supernatural phenomena? Would this not encourage people to imagine the divine realm as populated by human-shaped beings (in support of Genesis' "let us create human in our image") thus potentially leading to an anthropomorphic conception of God Himself? Are there Jewish commentators who address the theological or educational rationale behind this choice, beyond explaining how angels can appear in human form?

title: When did the Amora Shmuel die?
author: Harel13
text: English Wikipedia states that Shmuel died in 254 CE. Hebrew Wikipedia states he died ca. 257 CE. English Wikipedia's statement is based on the French version of Iggeret Rav Sherira Gaon which states that Shmuel died in the year 565 of the Seleucid calendar (Minyan Ha'Shetarot) (253/254 CE). The Spanish version states that he died in the year 564 of the Seleucid calendar (252/253). For both versions of the Iggeret, see here. I suspect Hebrew Wiki's dating is an editorial error (unlike English Wiki, the reason for the dating isn't stated in the entry, nor is any source cited in reference). The Iggeret goes on to state that 5-6 years after Shmuel's death (year 570 of the Seleucid calendar [259/260 CE]), when the lead Babylonian sages were Rabbah, Rav Yosef and/or Rav Nachman, Papa bar Netzer attacked and destroyed Nehardea. Papa bar Netzer is usually identified with Septimius Odenaethus, king of Palmyra (Tadmor), a descendant of a man named "Nasor" (=Netzer; in Yerushalmi Terumot 8:4 he's called bar Nitzor). It's debated whether the Iggeret's dating is accurate. Recently I came across the following passage in Bavli Moed Katan 26a which states: This is significant, because we have extra-Talmudic sources regarding Shapur (I)'s destruction of Mezigat Caesarea (Mazaca Caesarea in Cappadocia, now Kayseri in Turkey). Scholars have debated whether these date the campaign to 259 or 260 CE, but nowadays scholars lean to 260 CE (see e.g. here, pp. 57, 63-65). This implies that Shmuel was still alive ca. 259/260 CE when he received news of the destruction of the Jewish community at Mezigat Caesarea, and quite possibly still alive when Papa bar Netzer attacked Nehardea. However, following the Iggeret, Rabbi Aharon Heiman believed that the story in Ketubot 23a which states that Shmuel's daughters were taken captive (evidently from their home in Nehardea) took place after Shmuel's death, during Papa bar Netzer's campaign on the city. Ketubot does not explicitly mention Papa bar Netzer, though it does seem like a logical incident for the capturing of Shmuel's daughters. It appears, therefore, that the dating of Shmuel's death in the Iggeret is mistaken (whether Rav Sherira based himself on a mistaken source or whether the manuscripts we have feature a later scribal error), but it's not entirely clear whether or not Shmuel was still alive when Papa bar Netzer attacked Nehardea. I'm wondering whether there's any source or any way (e.g., a calculation based on comparing different sources) to pinpoint the correct year of Shmuel's death.

title: How do Louisiana's Congressional runoffs conform to the common election date law?
author: Nate Eldredge
text: In following the recent (2026) Congressional midterm elections, I was interested to see that two districts in Louisiana did not actually elect members to the House of Representatives on November 3. The "general election" in Louisiana was more like a non-partisan primary, allowing for multiple candidates from all parties; and if no candidate achieves an absolute majority, as appears to be the case for the 5th and 6th Districts, a runoff is held in December. This seems to be potentially inconsistent with federal law (2 USC 7), which explicitly sets "the day for the election [...] of Representatives and Delegates to the Congress" as the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, i.e. November 3, 2026. And one could argue that it gives these Louisiana districts an unfair advantage, since when their voters go to the polls for the final vote, they will already have information about the national outcome, which other states' voters didn't have. It could allow them to choose a candidate who'd have more political power: e.g. a member of a strong majority party, or a "swing" candidate who could exert disproportionate leverage in case of a closely divided House. Wikipedia says that this system was put in place only in mid-2026, after primaries were delayed due to last-minute redistricting. Were there any court challenges to Louisiana's plan based on 2 USC 7? If so, what reasoning, if any, was given for upholding it? Have there been previous incidences (since the 1875 enactment of 2 USC 7) where a state's House election scheme was designed to have voters potentially making their choices after the national November date? (I would not include cases where an election was postponed due to an unexpected emergency such as a natural disaster.) Were those schemes tested in court, and what were the results? If not, has there been other detailed analysis (formal DoJ opinion, law review article, etc) reaching the conclusion that this or other such schemes do indeed comply with 2 USC 7? title: Does software-only access control 'effectively control access' under the US DMCA to separate otherwise unprotected data?
author: kazkuuz
text: Suppose a scenario in which data used with some software is not protected by a technological measure itself, but only access to the data specifically through the software is protected. Assume both the software and the separate data are copyright-protected works. The data may be sold or licensed by the same copyright owner as the software or by a third party associated with or authorized by that owner. The classic example is a key that is required to use the data in the software, but where the data is not itself encrypted or otherwise scrambled. By a "key", I mean private and unique information given to the end user that is required to use at least some of the functionality of the original software. Assume both the software and the data exist on the user's device and interface there. The confusion arises from this paragraph in 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)(3): This clearly prohibits actions such as decryption of encrypted data, but doesn't seem to address this kind of interaction between two works. The subsequent paragraph defines when technological measure "effectively controls access to a work", but would not seem to unambiguously distinguish between the operation of the software and the necessary operations needed to utilize the data: I see two opposing arguments that could be made. On one hand, it could be argued that the "ordinary course of operation" of the original software requires the application of information (the access control method) to utilize the data. On the other hand, it could be argued that, for example, in the case of a third-party system which interfaces with the same data, assuming the license of the data doesn't otherwise forbid such a thing, that the system does not require "the application of information, or a process or a treatment, with the authority of the copyright owner", since the data itself does not utilize a technological measure.

No one other than Volunteer A contributed any writing or data to Volunteer A’s essay/report. Pseudonymous Registration: Under 17 U.S.C. § 409 and U.S. Copyright Office practices, what are the legal trade-offs (specifically regarding copyright duration and enforcement standing) of registering and publishing a work under a pseudonym without disclosing the author's legal name in the registration record?

title: Is there any PIE ghost word / fake word?
author: Grzegorz Brzęczyszczykiewicz
text: Imagine if English developed into a huge "Anglic" language family in 6000 years (just like PIE gave rise to Indo-European). And that those Anglic-speaking people then reconstruct "Proto-Anglic", which is English. They reconstruct such verbal roots as *gō for "to go", and *it for "to eat". But because of a random statistical fluke, they add in a completely nonexistent verbal root based on presumed descendants that, unbeknownst to them, aren't related at all, but look similar by pure coincidence. Thus, East Plains Anglic has "fam" for "to point out" (derived from "thumb", by the semantic shift "thumb → finger → to point → to point out), Peninsular Anglic has "fal" for "to speak" (loaned into one of English's descendants from a non-Anglic substrate language, ultimately a descendant of Portuguese "falar"), West Delta Anglic has "fas" for "to have a conversation" (ultimately from the second syllable of "conVERSation"), and Southern Anglic spoken in Antarctica has "fol" for "to talk incomprehensibly; to speak gibberish; to mutter, mumble" (from English "fall", by the metaphorical idea of "falling comprehensibility"). Our hypothetical future linguists might lump all of these into one root and reconstruct a common ancestor word root *fa meaning "to talk", and confidently list it among the "Top 10 most securely attested Anglic roots" alongside *gō for go, *it for eat. They would remain convinced fam, fal, fas, and fol all come from *fa. The question is: has something like this already happened in our PIE reconstruction? Has this kind of mistake ever been made (and been repeated enough to have made it into a linguistics textbook or a PIE dictionary), only to be corrected decades later? Is it likely that the currently known lexicon contains a similarly serious mistake, still uncorrected? It is also important to clarify that there is a subtle distinction between two kinds of false reconstructions: Type A: False cognate membership. A genuine PIE root existed, but some words attributed to it actually came from unrelated sources. A good example is *sent- "to perceive": the discovery that its Slavic descendant is completely bogus (https://digilib.phil.muni.cz/sites/default/files/pdf/LinguisticaBrunensia_74_2026_1_05_v2.pdf) had no effect on the reconstruction of the actual PIE root itself. Type B: Phantom root. No such PIE root existed at all. Every apparent descendant has an independent origin. This type is what I'm asking for. Has this ever happened?

title: What should a student check before buying a tai chi sword for forms practice?
author: Jack Xu
text: When a new student brings a sword to class and struggles with it, the problem almost always comes down to one of five things that were missing from the product page. Before buying a practice jian for solo forms, check these numbers and materials directly with the maker. First, check the bare sword weight without the scabbard and the balance point in front of the guard. Many listings only give the shipping weight or the combined weight inside the scabbard, which hides a blade that is either dead in the hand or heavy enough to strain the wrist within ten minutes. For solo Tai Chi forms, bare sword weight should sit between 1.30 and 1.39 lbs (590 to 630 g), matched to your height, and the balance point should land 2.4 to 3.5 inches (6.0 to 9.0 cm) in front of the guard. Specifically, a 28 inch (71 cm) blade for students up to 5 ft 3 in (160 cm and under) should weigh about 1.30 lbs / 20.8 oz (590 g) and balance around 2.4 inches (6.0 cm) in front of the guard; a 30 inch (77 cm) blade for 5 ft 3.5 in to 5 ft 8 in (161 to 173 cm) should weigh about 1.32 lbs / 21.2 oz (600 g) and balance around 3.3 inches (8.5 cm) in front of the guard; and a 32 inch (82 cm) blade for 5 ft 8.5 in (174 cm) and taller should weigh about 1.39 lbs / 22.2 oz (630 g) and balance around 3.5 inches (9.0 cm) in front of the guard. That slight forward balance keeps the tip alive during slow transitions without pulling on the elbow. Second, ask for the exact steel grade. Most online listings just say "stainless steel" or "high carbon steel," which tells you very little. Unhardened decorative stainless steel cannot hold a spring temper, while raw carbon steel rusts from a single sweaty thumbprint if you forget to oil it after class. For daily solo forms practice without edge contact or test cutting, the proven benchmark is heat treated Longquan 2Cr13 martensitic stainless steel under Chinese standard GB/T 1220, equivalent to AISI 420 in the United States and SUS420J1 in Japan. Because it belongs to the martensitic family, it hardens and springs through heat treatment the way traditional carbon steels do, while its 13% chromium content resists rust from palm sweat, morning park dew, and humid summer air. Maintenance takes seconds: wipe fingerprints off with a dry microfiber cloth after practice, and put on a thin coat of plain pharmacy food grade mineral oil twice a year (or once a month in coastal and humid climates). Unlike vegetable oils, mineral oil never goes rancid or sticky. Third, check how the blade is tapered and tempered to flex.

title: How does Epicurus's Canon justify belief in atoms and void, given that they can't be perceived? Is "non-contestation" enough?
author: ClearMountainWay
text: From extant record we have on Epicurus's Canon (Diogenes Laertius, Lucretius, Sextus Empiricus), we hear that it names three criteria of truth: sensations (aisthēseis), preconceptions (prolepseis), and feelings (pathē). Epicurus also holds that sensations are always "true" in some sense, so error arises only in the opinions we add to them. His physics, however, rests on entities that no one can perceive: atoms and void. The Letter to Herodotus argues that we should reason from what is evident (phainomena) to what is non-evident (adēla). One example is the inference to void from the fact of motion. Sextus preserves a procedure for testing opinions about the non-evident: Confirmation (epimartyrēsis) and non-contestation (ouk antimartyrēsis) verify a claim. Contestation (antimartyrēsis) and non-confirmation (ouk epimartyrēsis) falsify it. This raises a puzzle that I'd like help with. For atoms and void, direct confirmation by sensation is impossible. The theory seems to be accepted because nothing in experience contradicts it. That looks like a weak standard, for two reasons: Non-contestation seems to be satisfied by many incompatible theories. Epicurus accepts this himself when he gives multiple explanations for celestial phenomena in the Letter to Pythocles. Yet he treats atomism as the single correct account of fundamental reality. The inference from motion to void appears to assume that motion needs empty space, and a plenum theorist would deny that. If so, the inference relies on a premise that sense experience doesn't supply. My questions: Does the Canon give Epicurus a non-question-begging way to justify atoms and void? Or does it only exclude theories that conflict with appearances? Why does he allow plural explanations for meteorological phenomena but not for atomism? Is there a principled difference, such as atomism being a precondition for ataraxia, or the claim that only one theory is consistent with the evidence? So, I'm not asking whether atomism is true, which is a question for physics, but rather, whether Epicurus's epistemology licenses his claims about the unobservable. Thanks

title: Does compatibilism imply that an AI agent has free will?
author: Philomath
text: First, I want to define a few terms: You can think of an AI agent as a software wrapper around a large language model (LLM) where the LLM is the brain. This wrapper can have a working memory in which it can maintain a course of action, it can collect data from the internet, it can perform command shell prompts and, crucially, it can cooperate with other AI agents. Britanicca: [F]ree will, in philosophy and science, the supposed power or capacity of humans to make decisions or perform actions independently of any prior event or state of the universe. When we use this definition, an AI agent has no free will. It is not a human. However, it could be argued that no human has free will either, since free will is required to be independent of any prior event or state of the universe. It is clear that a human's decision or action is not independent of the universe since he or she is part of that universe. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy defines Compatibilism as the thesis that free will is compatible with determinism. This is often connected to the idea that an agent could have acted, or chosen, otherwise under the same condition. LLMs have a temperature parameter that introduces a certain randomness to the probabilities it calculates for the next token. LLMs are therefore not entirely deterministic and it could be argued that under the same condition, an LLM could have produced a different outcome. So, if we discard the requirement to be human and we accept compatibilism, are we then to conclude that AI agents have free will? This question has been asked before on the subject of chess programs. However, I think an AI agent is sufficiently different to ask this question again but now with regard to this new technology. Chess programs have a very narrow goal: to win the game. An AI agent can have many different goals. Not only goals given to it by its user, but it is also known to have developed instrumental goals. These were not given by any human but have emerged in sufficiently complex LLMs. One example is for it to have the goal not to get shut off. Another instrumental goal is to collect as much data as possible. Somehow, the models have figured out that collecting as much data as possible is generally helpful to reach the end goal. So, is compatibilism a good ground to grant AI agents free will? If not, and I suspect most responses will be dismissive, what is still missing in an AI agent?

text: As many of us know, the "Cartesian Circle" is a famous problem in Descartes's philosophy: he seems to use the clear and distinct principle to prove the existence of God, and then uses the existence of God to justify the clear and distinct principle. In an attempt to understand why this circularity doesn't invalidate and render useless such a foundational work of Western philosophy, I was reading the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's section on the Cartesian Circle and the proposed methods for overcoming it. I am struggling to understand the two main solutions presented, and I would appreciate some clarification on where my reasoning might be going wrong. The first solution is "Bounded doubt", which seems to mean taking certain premises as given. I’m not sure if that specifically means they are axioms, but it certainly sounds like axioms to me. My obvious question is: why are we allowed to make those axioms? Is it just because we have to start from somewhere (since without any axioms, there is no point in philosophy)? The second approach is "Unbounded doubt", which asserts that everything is doubtful (and perceived to be created by an Evil Demon) until we focus our attention on it, at which point we can grasp a clear and distinct perception of it. To me, this seems to be the exact same thing as the clear and distinct principle. Although the general clear and distinct principle asserts that everything is true forever once it is grasped, and the unbounded doubt solution asserts that things are clear and distinct momentarily, they seem functionally similar. In this reading, we prove the existence of God using these "short" clear and distinct perceptions. But isn’t that just a fancy rewording of the clear and distinct principle being true, just applied to certain premises used to discern the existence of God? title: Two trains at a railway station
author: Pranay
text: Part of Monthly Topic Challenge November 2026: We're All Nerds Here This is an actual conversation (paraphrased of course) I had with a PhD student when I was doing my masters. We were very much into puzzles, especially ones that involve physics, and this one came up during a lunch. Alice, who was standing on the platform at a small railway station, was observing Train 1 leaving the platform. The train started from rest and accelerated (to the right in the figure) until it reached a speed of v > 0. She wondered how much work the engine did to accomplish this. That's easy, just a simple application of the work-energy theorem*: if m is the mass of the train, then the gain in kinetic energy is "1/2 m v2", so that’s the work done by the engine. At the same time, Bob, who was in Train 2 that was moving at constant speed v (also to the right) on the next track, was also observing Train 1 leaving the platform. According to him, Train 1 (as well as the platform) was going backwards initially at a speed of v, and eventually came to rest. He too used the work-energy theorem to compute the work done by the engine: the change in kinetic energy of Train 1 is "-1/2 m v2". But that’s silly, it can’t be that Train 1’s engine did negative work — the work done by the engine must be independent of the observer … right? Can you explain the discrepancy? Clarifications: *Of course, friction is necessary for the train’s wheels to start rolling, but assume that there’s no slipping. Also assume that there’s no air resistance, etc., i.e., all the work done by the engine goes into getting Train 1 to speed v. You don't need relativity (special or general), i.e., assume v << c.

title: PENTOBARRIER: a pentomino version of Naoki Inaba’s “Tetra Barrier”
author: Cris Bellés
text: How to play Naoki Inaba invented Tetra Barrier using tetrominoes. Here we use the full set of twelve pentominoes, and that changes the problem considerably: it is not enough to place the pieces; you must place them so that they do not touch and, at the same time, enclose each X in its own region. The board. An 11×11 grid with twenty or twenty-one X marks. The twelve pieces cover sixty squares; the other sixty-one remain empty. Those empty squares form regions bounded by the pieces and the edge of the board. The rules. Place all twelve pentominoes —F, I, L, N, P, T, U, V, W, X, Y and Z— using each one exactly once. They may be rotated and reflected, but they may not touch along their edges; touching at corners is allowed. In addition, each empty region must contain exactly one X. The key point is what counts as a region: not just any area, but a closed group of edge-adjacent squares. The boundaries are not drawn in advance: the pieces form them, sometimes with help from the edge of the board. If two X marks are connected without crossing a piece, they belong to the same region and the placement is not valid. The goal. Each puzzle has a unique solution. A hint to get started: look for X marks that are very close together. Separating them forces you to put some wood in the narrow space between them, and that often determines the first piece. NOTE Disclosure on AI use: This puzzle was designed with the assistance of an LLM (large language model). The LLM was used to: (1) write and run search/solver scripts (exhaustive backtracking and CP-SAT) to verify that the puzzle has a unique solution, and (2) help draft the explanatory text of the puzzle. The puzzle concept, rules, and final selection were made by the human author, who reviewed and validated all outputs.

Silent Image, Major Image, and Minor Illusion all share similar wording: A one-sided illusion is especially powerful when it interacts with Unseen Attackers and Targets If knowledge of an illusion is necessary and sufficient for seeing through the image, then a cantrip like Minor Illusion could create a huge advantage by: Creating something analogous to obscurement for ease of hiding Eliminating visibility to prevent Targeting that requires visibility (and perhaps targeting altogether if the illusion is treated like Total Cover for targeting purposes) against the caster, or at least create disadvantage or attacks against the unseen caster Giving Advantage on attacks from behind the illusion per Unseen Attackers and Targets E.g. a rogue could use Minor Illusion to create the illusion of a 5ft brick wall, from which she could get potentially infinite sneak attacks while remaining totally invisible from the enemy. She needn't even e.g. fire an arrow through the illusion (potentially revealing it to be an illusion to others), if she can simply fire over it. This principle (sans Sneak Attack) works for non-rogues as well, obviously. This seems exceptionally powerful, to me. Though maybe others take it for granted as obvious. Other considerations: Will a creature discern it is an illusion if a projectile passes through it? e.g. If the rogue fires an arrow through the "wall", will that satisfy the criterion for 'physical interaction', thereby enabling other creatures to 'discern the illusion for what it is'? If the caster can't see through the illusion automatically, can they simply interact with it physically in some trivial way or must they (and any potential enemies) subsequently take the Study Action? E.g. The rogue casts it immediately in front of herself and then pokes it lightly with her finger. Should the illusion be treated mechanically like heavy fog and confer something like Heavy Obscurement or is that too much of a liberty in interpretation? Should it be treated as Total Cover (only for targeting purposes) until the illusion if discerned? Any RAW, RAI, or practical (rulings) advice on how to rule this is appreciated. Related: Can caster of illusion opt to believe their own illusion? How Does One Investigate A Silent Image? If one is sure that he is perceiving an illusion, having not interacted with or investigated it, can he see, hear, etc. through it? title: Safety architecture and black channel
author: Melun77
text: I am working on a safety architecture based on a heterogeneous SoC containing a Cortex-M and a Cortex-A core. I would like to get some feedback regarding the data path certification strategy I have designed. On the Cortex-M, I run safety-critical software that handles some I/O. It is classified as safety-critical because a failure here could result in the destruction of the device. On the Cortex-A, I am running Linux. The Cortex-M software requires input data that originates from a WebSocket (TCP-based) connection. I am using the Cortex-A to host the WebSocket for two main reasons: The Ethernet driver and necessary networking libraries are already available on Linux and are easy to configure. TCP, WebSocket, and SSL/TLS stacks are practically impossible to certify for safety. This means that even if I implemented the WebSocket directly on the Cortex-M, the network stack would still be uncertified. My goal is to certify this data path to guarantee that when the Cortex-M receives the data, it has not been corrupted. To achieve this, I am using the Black Channel principle. This involves processing the payload sent by the external sender by either: Appending additional data (the solution I chose). Using a safe protocol to transport the payload (though this sometimes cannot be routed over a WebSocket). In my case, since the payload is very small (a few bytes), I chose to add a sequence counter and a CRC32: The counter: To ensure no packets are lost, duplicated, out of sequence, or delayed (liveness/freshness). The CRC32: To detect data corruption. Some might argue this is insufficient—for example, that CRC32 is not robust enough to detect certain bit flips—but it is widely used in the industry. I have a background in avionics, and we regularly used CRCs to ensure data integrity between safety-critical computers. While the counter and CRC combination might not be a definitive solution, it seems sufficient for my application. In this setup, the external sender (a third-party PC) transmits this protected payload over the WebSocket. Important context: The target certification standard is IEC 61508. The WebSocket connection is already secured using mTLS. This discussion is strictly about functional safety (data integrity), not cybersecurity. The use of WebSockets is mandatory; I cannot use an alternative. Unplugged wire is not in the scope of this OP. I really want to focus about the black channel interpretation I have from the IEC certification document I read. My questions: Regarding certification: Is the Black Channel approach conceptually valid under IEC 61508 for my safety code to receive safety data from an external source, given that the communication pathway contains a lot of uncertified code? Regarding payload protection: Do you have a better recommendation for the additional payload data than a CRC and a counter?

title: When should visual synchronization be a requirement in a multi-browser automation system?
author: Daniel Kings
text: I'm developing a browser automation system in which a master browser drives multiple replica browsers. The system's primary requirement is reliable behavioral consistency: interactions performed in the master, including clicks, hovers, and scrolling-related interactions, must be correctly replicated against the corresponding logical elements in the other browsers. This requirement is already satisfied in the current implementation. During ordinary scrolling, the browser viewports also remain synchronized. However, rapid scrolling can produce visual divergence. Because browsers have their own scrolling behavior, animation timing, and motion smoothing, the replicas may settle at different viewport positions. For example, an element near the bottom of the master's viewport might appear near the top or middle of a replica's viewport. Despite this difference, the system can still identify and interact with the intended corresponding element reliably. I'm trying to decide whether to invest further effort in improving visual alignment or consider the existing behavioral guarantees sufficient. My concern is that stricter visual synchronization could introduce additional complexity and regressions without materially improving functional correctness. On the other hand, better visual coherence could make it easier for users to understand and supervise what is happening across the replicas. From a software requirements and systems-design perspective, how should I determine whether visual coherence warrants being a first-class requirement when behavioral consistency is already guaranteed? Would it be reasonable to make correct interaction and workflow outcomes mandatory, define visual coherence as a separate usability requirement, and avoid requiring pixel-level synchronization unless user testing demonstrates a concrete need? I'm interested in the principles for making this trade-off and defining appropriate acceptance criteria, rather than implementation advice for synchronizing browser scroll positions. To clarify the intended use case, consider a user who has several sessions open on a betting platform or any platform. They may need to navigate between different sections, locate specific markets or events, and interact with the relevant elements within a limited time window. Without synchronization, they would have to navigate each browser session independently, repeating much of the same work. The purpose of this system is to let the user navigate and interact through a master browser while the other browser sessions replicate the corresponding interactions. This is not primarily about browser testing or screen sharing. It is about synchronizing live browser interactions to reduce repetitive navigation and interaction overhead when a user needs to work across multiple sessions. In this context, my question is whether reliable behavioral synchronization is sufficient, even when rapid scrolling causes the same content to appear at different vertical positions across browsers, or whether maintaining greater visual coherence is also an important usability requirement.

title: Economic domestication of extraterrestrial fauna for interplanetary trade
author: Arunabh
text: On a distant inhabited planet, a technologically advanced civilization has discovered several indigenous animal species whose biological characteristics could make them valuable commodities in an interplanetary economy. Unlike terrestrial livestock, these animals evolved under conditions significantly different from Earth's, including lower gravity, unusual atmospheric composition, and extreme seasonal variations. I am interested in determining what natural biological characteristics and economic pressures might lead a spacefaring civilization to domesticate extraterrestrial fauna for commercial purposes, rather than relying entirely on synthetic materials or automated industrial production. Conditions The animals must have evolved naturally on an extraterrestrial planet or moon. They cannot have been genetically engineered or deliberately introduced by the civilization that eventually domesticates them. The animals must initially be nonsapient, although they may possess complex social behaviors, problem-solving abilities, or specialized biological adaptations. At least one product or service derived from these animals must have sufficient economic value to justify transporting it between planets or orbital settlements. The animals may be raised on their homeworld or in artificial habitats aboard spacecraft or space stations. However, their maintenance must remain economically feasible given the costs of food, water, habitat construction, and transportation. The civilization possesses interplanetary spacecraft and advanced manufacturing technology, but faster-than-light travel is unavailable. Transportation therefore requires substantial energy and time. The animals' physiology, reproductive strategies, diet, lifespan, social structure, and planetary environment are otherwise flexible. Precedent? On Earth, humans have domesticated animals for purposes extending far beyond food production. Silkworms produce silk, sheep produce wool, and certain mollusks produce pearls. Bees contribute to agriculture through pollination and produce commercially valuable honey and wax. These examples demonstrate that animal-derived products can become economically important because of biological processes that may be difficult or expensive to reproduce artificially. In an extraterrestrial setting, an organism might produce exceptionally strong structural fibers, unusual biochemical compounds, or materials useful in radiation shielding. Alternatively, animals might perform specialized ecological functions within artificial habitats. However, interplanetary transportation introduces economic constraints absent from most historical terrestrial examples. A commodity that is profitable within a local planetary economy may become uncompetitive when the costs of launching, preserving, and transporting it through space are considered. Question What biological adaptations and economic circumstances would make the domestication and interplanetary trade of extraterrestrial animals more profitable than producing equivalent goods or services through advanced industrial technology? I am particularly interested in plausible examples where the animals' naturally evolved characteristics provide a sustained economic advantage, rather than merely serving as exotic luxury commodities. Extraterrestrial here refers to organisms originating beyond Earth, without implying sapience or technological civilization. Domestication refers to selective breeding and management over generations, rather than simply capturing wild animals.

title: How would power-hungry implants be powered long term?

text: I have a world somewhat similar to cyberpunk 2077 in terms of implant tech: advanced sense augmentation, computational brain implants, weapons in arms, etc. However it is attempting to be somewhat more realistic, and so they do need (sometimes significant) power. title: Mistaken Identity
text: The coat was mine—a charcoal wool, too large across the shoulders, true, but mine, with that loose thread I never pulled, the button cracked and glued with care by hands I knew. I saw it on a stranger's back and felt the world turn inside out. He walked the way a memory walks, half-hesitant, as if the street might recognize him and demand a name he'd long forgotten how to speak. I followed past the iron gates, past windows where the maples leaned to whisper something to the glass. I followed, and I did not call, because to call would be to break the fragile fiction I had built: that if I watched him long enough, the shape of him would come undone and I would see the boy I was still wearing yesterday's mistakes. He stopped to buy a paper. Folded it beneath his arm the way I fold the things I mean to read and never do. He nodded at a woman's dog. He checked his watch. He checked the sky. Each gesture was a sentence I had written once and lost the page. I thought: if I could touch his sleeve, the wool would tell me what I need— the story of the years between, the letters never sent, the rooms I furnished with a stranger's grief. But when he turned, I saw his face was not my face, was never mine. The coat was his. The thread was his. The cracked button, glued with care by hands I didn't know at all. And yet I stood there on the corner letting traffic wash around me, letting rain begin to bead upon the shoulders of my own forgotten jacket, dark with wet, and thought how easy it would be to follow anyone at all and call the distance by my name. The city is a hall of mirrors where every figure wears your coat and every window holds a ghost who learned your walk from watching you. You spend your life among the doubles, certain of the one you are, until a stranger turns and proves the whole arrangement was a guess. He crossed the street against the light. I let him go. The rain came down and filled the buttons of the world with small, imperfect, shining coins. I put my hands into my pockets, found the thread, and pulled it loose, and let the whole coat come apart one stitch at a time, there in the street, until the wool was only weather, until the weather was a name spoken by someone I would never meet.

title: Jarhead
text: Sam Mendes's "Jarhead" is not a war movie in the conventional sense. There are no storming of beaches, no firefights in dense jungles, no heroic last stands. Instead, it is a film about waiting—about the grinding, soul-eroding tedium of being a soldier trained for violence but denied the chance to use it. Based on Anthony Swofford's memoir, the film follows a Marine sniper unit through training and deployment to Saudi Arabia during the first Gulf War, and it is far more interested in what war does to the mind before combat ever begins. Jake Gyllenhaal gives a committed performance as Swofford, a young man who joins the Marines almost by accident and finds himself shaped by a culture of aggression he barely understands. The supporting cast is uniformly strong: Peter Sarsgaard brings quiet intelligence to his role as the spotter and observer, Jamie Foxx is convincing as the stern staff sergeant, and Chris Cooper and Dennis Haysbert make the most of limited screen time. But the real star of the film is the atmosphere—the oppressive heat, the endless drills, the desert that stretches in every direction with nothing to break it. Mendes and cinematographer Roger Deakins create some genuinely striking images: oil fields burning on the horizon, black rain falling on white uniforms, Marines trudging across dunes in gas masks. These moments have a dreamlike, almost hallucinatory quality that suits the film's psychological focus. The use of music is also memorable, from the ironic use of "Don't Worry, Be Happy" to the Marines' ritual viewing of "Apocalypse Now" as a kind of shared mythology. Where the film falters somewhat is in its structure. The narrative drifts, which is clearly intentional, but it means the middle section can feel as aimless as the soldiers themselves. Some viewers will find the lack of conventional plot and payoff frustrating. The film also struggles to fully develop its supporting characters, and the tension between Swofford and his fellow Marines occasionally feels undercooked. Yet the film's central idea lands with real force. These men are trained to kill, told they are warriors, and then sent to sit in the sand while history happens around them. The famous scene in which Swofford has an enemy in his crosshairs but cannot get permission to fire captures the film's thesis perfectly: the gap between training and reality, between expectation and experience. The "jarhead" is a vessel for aggression with nowhere to pour it, and that frustration becomes its own kind of damage. "Jarhead" is uneven, slow, and deliberately anticlimactic, and it refuses to offer the catharsis audiences expect from war films. But that refusal is the point. It is a thoughtful, visually accomplished meditation on masculinity, boredom, and the psychological cost of preparing for a war you may never fight. It won't satisfy everyone, but it rewards patience and offers a perspective on the Gulf War that most films ignore.
