title: Dried Fruit Poached in Port
text: Dried Fruit Poached in Port A bowl of dried fruit poached in port is one of the quietest, most comforting desserts I know. It asks almost nothing of the cook — no whisking, no timing, no temperamental oven — yet it rewards you with something that tastes of deep winter luxury. The fruit plumps into soft, wine-dark jewels, the syrup turns glossy and fragrant, and the whole thing can be made days ahead. Serve it warm with a spoonful of thick cream, or cold with a slice of plain cake, or even over morning porridge if you are feeling generous with yourself. The beauty of this recipe is its flexibility. Use whatever dried fruit you have — a mix of prunes, apricots, figs, raisins, sultanas, and dates works beautifully. I like to keep the fruit fairly large so it retains some bite; a prune left whole or an apricot halved will soften without collapsing. If you have candied orange peel or a few strips of fresh zest, add them. A cinnamon stick is lovely, but so is a star anise or a couple of cloves. The port itself does most of the work, so choose one you would be happy to drink — a ruby or tawny both work, though ruby gives a fruitier, more vivid syrup. Begin with 500g of mixed dried fruit. If any pieces are very large, cut them in half. Place the fruit in a medium saucepan and add 400ml of port, 200ml of water, 3 tablespoons of honey or light brown sugar, the zest of one orange (in wide strips, avoiding the bitter white pith), and one cinnamon stick. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, then reduce the heat to low so the liquid barely bubbles. Cover and cook for 20 minutes, stirring once or twice, until the fruit is plump and tender but not mushy. The timing will vary depending on the fruit — figs and dates take longer than raisins — so check at 15 minutes and continue in 5-minute increments as needed. Uncover the pan and simmer for another 5 to 10 minutes, until the liquid has reduced to a light syrup that coats the fruit. Do not let it reduce too far; it will thicken further as it cools. Taste and add a squeeze of lemon juice if the syrup seems too sweet, or a splash more port if it needs lift. Remove the cinnamon stick and orange zest. Let the fruit cool in the syrup for at least 20 minutes before serving. It will keep, covered and refrigerated, for up to two weeks, and the flavour improves after a day or two. Serve warm or at room temperature, with the syrup spooned over. A dollop of crème fraîche, a scoop of vanilla ice cream, or a slice of toasted brioche all make fine companions. Serves six to eight, depending on how greedy everyone is.

title: Crazy
text: The neighbor’s dog barks at a leaf that fell three hours ago, and will not stop. My mother irons the same shirt again, the crease already sharp enough to cut. This is the house where nothing happens twice and everything repeats. I knew a man who built a boat inside his basement, thirty years, a hull too wide to fit the door. He said the sea would find him anyway. He said the water table underneath the town was rising, and he wasn’t wrong. There is a woman on the corner who counts the cars that turn left, keeping score in a notebook only she can read. She has a system. She has her reasons. Once I asked her what the numbers meant, and she looked at me the way you’d look at someone who had never learned to read. The trick is not to call it by its name. The trick is to keep the edges soft. The man who talks to pigeons in the square is not disturbed—he is in conversation. The woman who saves every newspaper is not hoarding—she is remembering what the rest of us let go. I have a drawer of keys that fit no lock. I have a habit of checking the stove a dozen times before I sleep. The dog still barks. The iron still steams. The boat still waits beneath the floor. We are all of us a little wrong, a little tuned to stations no one else can hear. The trick is to keep the dial turned low, to hum along with what we cannot name, to let the static be a kind of music. So let the neighbor’s dog go on. Let the woman count. Let the man in his basement sand the hull until his hands are smooth as water. Let the pigeons answer back. The world is full of people carrying their own weather, their own small compasses pointing somewhere north of sense. And still the sun comes up. And still the morning makes its rounds. I check the stove. I check it twice. I check it three times, then I sleep, and in my sleep I dream of boats, of basements filling slowly with the tide, of numbers that at last add up to something like a life. The dog has stopped. The leaf is still. The woman has gone home to write it down. Somewhere a man is painting hulls the color of a sea he’s never seen. Somewhere a notebook fills with light. We are not broken. We are tuned to frequencies that others miss. We are the static and the song. We are the crease that will not flatten, the key that turns in no one’s hand, the boat that waits, and waits, and waits for water that is surely coming.

text: Audrey Tautou's latest film, the romantic comedy Hors de Prix (Priceless), leads the nominations for France's most prestigious film awards, the Cesars, with five nods. Also in the running for best picture is the thriller Ne le dis à personne (Tell No One), Guillaume Canet's adaptation of Harlan Coben's novel, which earned seven nominations. The fifth best picture nominee is Quand j'étais chanteur (When I Was a Singer), Xavier Giannoli's drama about a fading dance-hall crooner, which earned six nominations including best actor for Gérard Depardieu. text: The US dollar slipped against most major currencies on Monday as traders closed out the year by reducing safe-haven holdings, with thin holiday trading magnifying price moves. The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of six peers, fell 0.4%, while the euro rose 0.5% and sterling gained 0.3%. The yen also strengthened, pushing the dollar down 0.6% against the Japanese currency. Market participants said the move reflected a broader rebalancing of portfolios before the end of the year rather than a single piece of economic news. With many desks operating on skeleton staff and several major markets closed or closing early, even modest flows had an outsized effect. "Liquidity is very poor, so it does not take much to move the dollar," said one currency strategist at a European bank. The greenback had been supported for much of the year by expectations that the Federal Reserve would keep interest rates higher for longer than other major central banks. In Europe, the euro found support from a modest improvement in risk appetite and from expectations that the European Central Bank may be slower to cut rates than some investors had feared. The pound was helped by year-end demand for sterling, though analysts cautioned that the UK economy's outlook remained fragile. title: Laal Mass (Fiery Lamb Curry)
text: Laal Mass (Fiery Lamb Curry) Laal Mass, literally "red meat," is the crown jewel of Rajasthani cuisine—a dish as fierce and unyielding as the desert from which it hails. Born in the royal kitchens of Rajputana, this curry derives its signature scarlet hue not from tomatoes or artificial colouring, but from the generous use of dried red chillies, which also lend it a magnificent, slow-building heat. Unlike richer Mughlai curries, Laal Mass is deliberately stark: no onions, no tomatoes, no cream. Just meat, fat, chillies, and a handful of whole spices. The result is a curry of startling clarity and intensity, where the lamb itself is the star. Traditionally, Laal Mass is made with mutton—goat meat, preferably from the leg or shoulder, cut into large bone-in chunks. The bones are essential; they give the gravy its body and depth. The meat should be fatty, as the fat carries the chilli's heat and the spices' fragrance. Serves 4–6. Ingredients: 1 kg bone-in mutton or lamb, cut into 2-inch pieces 10–12 dried Kashmiri red chillies (for colour) 4–6 dried spicy red chillies (such as Guntur or Byadagi), adjust to your tolerance 1 cup full-fat yoghurt, whisked smooth 4 tablespoons mustard oil or ghee 1 teaspoon cumin seeds 4 green cardamom pods 2 black cardamom pods 1 cinnamon stick 4 cloves 1 teaspoon black peppercorns 1 tablespoon ginger paste 1 tablespoon garlic paste 1 teaspoon turmeric powder 1 teaspoon coriander powder Salt to taste 2 cups hot water Fresh coriander leaves, to garnish Method: Begin by preparing the chillies. Remove their stems and soak them in half a cup of hot water for twenty minutes. Drain, reserving the soaking liquid, and blend the chillies with a little water into a smooth, thick paste. Set aside. Pat the mutton dry and season lightly with salt. Heat the mustard oil in a heavy-bottomed pot or pressure cooker until it shimmers and just begins to smoke—this removes its raw pungency. Reduce the heat to medium. Add the cumin seeds, green and black cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, and peppercorns. Let them sizzle for thirty seconds until fragrant. Add the ginger and garlic pastes and cook, stirring, for a minute until the raw smell disappears. Now add the mutton and sear it well on all sides, turning the pieces until they are browned and coated in the aromatics—about eight to ten minutes. Sprinkle in the turmeric, coriander powder, and salt. Lower the heat and add the whisked yoghurt, one spoonful at a time, stirring continuously to prevent curdling. Cook for five minutes until the yoghurt is absorbed and the meat takes on a pale golden colour. Stir in the chilli paste and cook for another five minutes, allowing the raw edge of the chillies to mellow. The pot will smell potent—this is as it should be.

title: Cecil Weir
text: Cecil Weir (1890–1950) was a British engineer and industrialist best known for his work in the development of early radio broadcasting equipment and his later contributions to the British electronics industry. Over a career spanning four decades, Weir held several patents relating to valve (vacuum tube) design and wireless transmission, and served as a technical adviser to the BBC during its formative years. Early life and education Weir was born in Glasgow, Scotland, on 14 March 1890, the second son of a shipbuilding draughtsman. He attended Allan Glen's School before winning a scholarship to study electrical engineering at the Royal Technical College (later the University of Strathclyde). He graduated in 1911 and took a position with the Clyde Valley Electrical Power Company, where he worked on high-voltage transmission systems. Career With the outbreak of the First World War, Weir joined the Royal Engineers Signal Service, where he was assigned to wireless telegraphy units. His wartime work on improving trench radio sets brought him into contact with engineers at the Marconi Company, and in 1919 he joined Marconi's research department at Chelmsford. At Marconi, Weir worked under Charles Samuel Franklin on directional antenna design and the development of transmitting valves. He was granted his first patent in 1921 for a method of stabilizing oscillator circuits, a problem that had limited the reliability of early broadcast transmitters. In 1923 he was appointed chief engineer of the newly formed Wireless Equipment Company, a Marconi subsidiary supplying receivers to the expanding civilian market. Weir's most significant contribution came during the establishment of the British Broadcasting Company. Between 1923 and 1925 he served as a consulting engineer to the company, advising on transmitter siting and the design of the chain of medium-wave stations that provided the first near-national radio coverage. He advocated the use of synchronized transmitters operating on a common wavelength, an approach later adopted for the BBC's regional service. In 1926 Weir left Marconi to found Weir Instruments Ltd, a firm based in Slough that manufactured laboratory oscilloscopes, signal generators, and precision components for the valve industry. The company prospered during the 1930s, supplying equipment to universities and to the Admiralty. Weir served as managing director until 1948. Later life During the Second World War, Weir Instruments converted to war production, manufacturing radar components under contract to the Ministry of Supply. Weir acted as a technical liaison between the firm and the Telecommunications Research Establishment. He retired in 1948 owing to ill health and died at his home in Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, on 2 November 1950, survived by his wife, Margaret, and two daughters. Legacy Weir is remembered chiefly for his role in the technical groundwork of British broadcasting and for the instrument company that bore his name, which continued to operate under successive owners until the 1980s. A collection of his papers and patent specifications is held by the Institution of Engineering and Technology archives in London.

title: The Revenant
text: Alejandro González Iñárritu's *The Revenant* is less a traditional survival thriller than a sensory assault, a brutal and often beautiful meditation on endurance, vengeance, and the thin line between man and beast. Loosely based on the life of frontiersman Hugh Glass, the film follows Leonardo DiCaprio's trapper through a frozen American wilderness after he is mauled by a grizzly bear and left for dead by his fellow men—most notably the ruthless John Fitzgerald, played with venomous conviction by Tom Hardy. What unfolds is a nearly wordless odyssey of suffering and determination, shot with staggering technical ambition by Emmanuel Lubezki, whose continuous, roving camera work creates an almost unbearable immediacy. The film's greatest strength is its immersive craft. Lubezki's natural-light photography captures the frontier with an elemental grandeur: misted forests, rushing rivers, and snowbound plains feel at once majestic and hostile. The infamous bear attack sequence is a masterclass in visceral filmmaking—chaotic, terrifying, and painfully prolonged, it sets the tone for a world where violence is sudden and indifferent. Iñárritu's decision to shoot in remote locations with long, unbroken takes lends the proceedings a documentary-like authenticity, though at times the stylistic flourishes border on self-conscious artistry. There are moments when the camera's lingering gaze on suffering feels less like storytelling and more like spectacle. DiCaprio's performance is the film's emotional anchor. Working with minimal dialogue, he communicates Glass's pain, grief, and stubborn will through physicality—crawling through mud, gnawing raw flesh, and staring into the void with haunted eyes. It is a committed, punishing turn, though one could argue the role demands more endurance than emotional range. Hardy provides a compelling counterpoint as the paranoid, survivalist Fitzgerald, whose pragmatic cruelty makes him a worthy antagonist. The supporting cast, including Domhnall Gleeson and Will Poulter, is solid, though the film's sparse dialogue and relentless forward momentum leave little room for character depth. Where *The Revenant* falters is in its thematic reach. The screenplay, co-written by Iñárritu and Mark L. Smith, gestures toward grand ideas—man versus nature, the cyclical nature of violence, the possibility of redemption—but rarely explores them with nuance. Glass's recurring visions of his deceased wife feel like heavy-handed symbolism, and the film's treatment of Native American characters, while sympathetic, leans on familiar tropes of noble suffering. The revenge narrative, meanwhile, is straightforward to the point of predictability; the destination is never in doubt, only the grueling journey. Yet that journey is the point, and on a purely cinematic level, *The Revenant* is often breathtaking. The sound design—howling winds, cracking ice, labored breathing—wraps around the viewer like a frozen shroud. The film's portrayal of the fur trade era is grimly convincing, a world of mud, blood, and casual brutality. At over two and a half hours, it occasionally drags, particularly in the middle stretch, but the cumulative impact is undeniable. Ultimately, *The Revenant* is an experience to be endured as much as admired. It is a film of immense technical skill and genuine ambition, anchored by a fearless performance from its lead.

title: I2C SDA line acts erratically, requiring touch to work
text: I'm working on a small sensor board built around an STM32F103 (blue pill clone) acting as an I2C master, talking to a BME280 breakout at 100 kHz over a short run of jumper wires (about 10 cm). The pull-ups are 4.7 kΩ to 3.3 V on both SDA and SCL. Everything is powered from the same 3.3 V LDO, and the grounds are common. The problem: most of the time, communication fails outright. HAL_I2C_IsDeviceReady() returns HAL_ERROR, and if I scope the lines, SDA sits low while SCL idles high. It looks like SDA is being held low continuously, as though some device is stuck mid-transfer or the master isn't releasing the line. Interestingly, if I touch the SDA line with my finger (or press a finger across both SDA and the adjacent GND pad on the breakout), the bus suddenly starts working and stays working for a while, sometimes for minutes. After it fails again, another touch brings it back. This is completely reproducible. What I've tried so far: Swapped the BME280 breakout for a second identical unit — same behavior. Changed the pull-ups from 10 kΩ down to 4.7 kΩ, then to 2.2 kΩ — no real change. Shortened the wires to ~5 cm, twisted SDA with GND — slightly better, but still fails. Verified with a multimeter that SCL and SDA both idle at 3.3 V when the board is powered but before HAL_I2C_Init() is called. After init and the first failed transaction, SDA is stuck near 0.4 V. Added a 100 nF decoupling cap on the breakout's VCC — no effect. Tried slowing the bus to 50 kHz and even 10 kHz — still fails the same way. Confirmed the STM32's I2C pins are configured as open-drain alternate function, and that I'm not accidentally driving SDA push-pull. Added HAL_I2C_DeInit() / HAL_I2C_Init() recovery, plus the standard "clock out 9 pulses on SCL" bus-recovery routine before each transaction. The recovery sometimes helps, but not reliably, and it doesn't explain why a finger touch changes anything. Checked that the BME280's SDO pin is tied to a defined level (GND, giving address 0x76). Measured the pull-up voltage at the breakout with a scope: it looks clean, though when SDA is stuck low there's a visible ~1.5 V plateau on the rising edge of SCL, suggesting something is fighting the pull-up. The finger-touch dependency is what confuses me most. Touching SDA adds maybe a few tens of picofarads of body capacitance to ground, which should make the edges *worse*, not better, so I doubt it's a rise-time issue. It behaves more like the touch is bleeding off a stuck charge or providing a weak pull-down/pull-up path that lets the line escape a latched state. I've also noticed that if I touch the metal shield of the USB connector instead, it usually does *not* fix it, so it seems specific to the SDA net rather than general ESD/grounding weirdness.

text: I volunteered with a small environmental nonprofit for about eight months. I was never an employee, never signed anything, and was never paid. I did the work on my own time, using my own computer, and I was not given any materials from the organization beyond a few public documents and some internal notes they shared with me. I produced a substantial report — around 40 pages — with original analysis, citations, and recommendations. I sent a draft to the director and we discussed it a couple of times. They gave feedback and asked for changes, which I made. Near the end, I sent what I considered a final version. I did not include any copyright notice, and I did not register anything. The organization later posted a PDF of the report on its website with my name as author, and also used excerpts in grant applications and in comments submitted to a government agency. I was fine with that at the time; I understood my role as helping the cause. I never assigned or transferred anything in writing, and no one ever said “this belongs to us” or “you retain rights” or anything similar. I now want to publish the report myself, possibly through a small independent press, and maybe adapt parts of it into articles. I was an unpaid volunteer, not an employee, and there was no written agreement. Does the work-for-hire doctrine apply to volunteers at all, or only employees and certain specially commissioned works under 17 U.S.C. § 101? Does it matter that the director suggested the topic and gave feedback, versus me choosing the topic and doing all the drafting? 2. If I own the copyright, did I grant the organization an implied nonexclusive license to use the report as they have (website posting, grant excerpts, regulatory comments)?

title: Did the post-resurrection flesh-and-bone body of Jesus change into a spiritual, incorporeal, and non-tangible body when he was taken in the clouds?
text: In Luke 24:39, the risen Jesus invites the disciples to touch him, saying, "a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have." John 20:27 likewise records Jesus telling Thomas to put his finger into the nail marks and his hand into his side. These texts are commonly taken to establish that the resurrection body of Jesus was physical, tangible, and continuous with the body that was crucified. Yet other passages seem to point in a different direction. In 1 Corinthians 15:44–50, Paul contrasts the "natural body" (sōma psychikon) with the "spiritual body" (sōma pneumatikon), and states that "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God." In 1 Peter 3:18, Christ is said to have been "put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit." And in 2 Corinthians 3:17, "the Lord is the Spirit." Some interpreters, reading these together with the ascension and the language of Jesus being "taken up" in a cloud (Acts 1:9), conclude that the tangible, flesh-and-bone appearances were only temporary accommodations, and that when Jesus was taken into the clouds—or at some point between the resurrection and the ascension—his body was transformed into a spiritual, incorporeal, and non-tangible mode of existence. My question concerns the timing and nature of that alleged change. Specifically: does Scripture teach that the post-resurrection flesh-and-bone body of Jesus changed into a spiritual, incorporeal, and non-tangible body when he was taken up in the clouds? Several sub-questions bear on this: 1. The meaning of "spiritual body" (sōma pneumatikon). Does Paul's phrase in 1 Corinthians 15:44 denote a body that is immaterial and non-tangible, or does it denote a body animated and governed by the Spirit, still corporeal but transformed in its properties (as the "natural body" is animated by the soul)? The fact that Paul still calls it a sōma is significant, but I would like to see how this is handled by those who take the incorporeal view. 2. The continuity of the appearances. If the change occurred at the ascension, how do we account for the fact that the appearances during the forty days were already described as strange and discontinuous with ordinary bodily life—appearing behind locked doors (John 20:19, 26), vanishing from sight (Luke 24:31), and not always being immediately recognized (Luke 24:16; John 20:14; 21:4)? Conversely, if the change occurred at the resurrection itself, how do we account for the explicit flesh-and-bone language and the eating of broiled fish (Luke 24:42–43)? 3. The ascension and the cloud. Does the cloud in Acts 1:9 signify a change of nature, or is it merely the visible means by which he departed from their sight? Does "taken up" imply removal from the earthly sphere rather than a change from tangible to intangible? 4. The nature of Christ's present session. Related to this, does the New Testament anywhere describe the presently exalted Christ as incorporeal or non-tangible?

title: Army of Darkness
text: Sam Raimi’s *Army of Darkness* is a glorious, blood-soaked, and unapologetically campy masterpiece of genre filmmaking that serves as the high-octane conclusion to the *Evil Dead* trilogy. While its predecessor, *Evil Dead II*, perfected the blend of slapstick comedy and visceral horror, *Army of Darkness* pivots toward something entirely different: a swashbuckling, medieval fantasy epic viewed through a fractured, Looney Tunes lens. It is a film that understands the inherent joy of absurdity, trading the claustrophobic dread of a cabin in the woods for the wide-open, chaotic battlefields of a distorted past. At the heart of this madness is Bruce Campbell, who delivers what is arguably the definitive performance of his career as Ash Williams. By this stage in the trilogy, Ash has evolved from a terrified victim into a reluctant, chin-forward action hero. He is the quintessential "everyman" thrust into a world of sorcery and skeletons, armed with nothing but a chainsaw for a hand and a double-barreled shotgun. Campbell’s charisma is the engine that drives the entire production; his ability to pivot from deadpan sarcasm to over-the-top bravado allows the film to maintain its manic energy without ever losing its sense of character. He doesn't just play a hero; he plays a hero who is frequently confused, frustrated, and wildly out of his depth, which makes his eventual triumphs all the more entertaining. Visually, the film is a feast of kinetic energy. Raimi’s signature "shaky cam" and inventive POV shots are in full effect, turning even the simplest movement into a frantic, sensory experience. The production design, despite its modest budget, manages to create a world that feels lived-in and textured, even if that world is populated by deadites with exaggerated, grotesque features. The practical effects are a standout, utilizing stop-motion animation, puppetry, and heavy prosthetic makeup to create a sense of tangible, tactile horror that CGI simply cannot replicate. There is a weight to the gore and a physicality to the combat that makes the film’s more ridiculous moments feel strangely grounded in their own internal logic. The tonal shift from horror to adventure is handled with a playful touch. While some purists may miss the genuine tension of the original films, *Army of Darkness* succeeds because it leans fully into its identity as a cult comedy. It mocks the tropes of heroic fantasy even as it celebrates them. The dialogue is snappy, the pacing is relentless, and the musical score adds a sense of grandiosity that perfectly parodies the epic cinema of the era. Ultimately, *Army of Darkness* is a film made with pure, unadulterated passion. It is a celebration of B-movie aesthetics and a testament to the idea that filmmaking can be, above all else, immensely fun. It doesn't ask for your intellectual respect; it asks for your undivided attention and your willingness to laugh at the absurdity of it all.

title: Potato Gnocchi in Lemon-Butter Sauce with Scallops and Sea Urchin
text: This dish is a study in coastal luxury, balancing the earthy, pillowy texture of handmade potato gnocchi with the briny, creamy decadence of sea urchin (uni) and the delicate sear of diver scallops. The lemon-butter sauce acts as the bridge, providing acidity to cut through the richness while highlighting the natural sweetness of the seafood. Yields: 2 servings Prep time: 1 hour (plus potato drying time) Cook time: 20 minutes Ingredients For the Potato Gnocchi: 1 lb Russet potatoes (starchy is essential) 1 ½ cups Type 00 flour (plus extra for dusting) 1 large egg, lightly beaten ½ tsp fine sea salt A pinch of freshly grated nutmeg For the Seafood: 6 large U-10 Diver Scallops, patted extremely dry 3–4 oz high-quality fresh Sea Urchin (Uni) 2 tbsp high-smoke point oil (grapeseed or avocado) 1 tbsp unsalted butter (for searing) For the Lemon-Butter Sauce: 4 tbsp unsalted European-style butter, cubed and chilled Juice and zest of ½ organic lemon ¼ cup dry white wine (Pinot Grigio or Sauvignon Blanc) 1 small shallot, minced fine 2 tbsp pasta water (reserved from boiling gnocchi) Fresh micro-greens or chives for garnish Flaky sea salt (Maldon) Instructions 1. Prepare the Gnocchi: Begin by boiling the whole, unpeeled potatoes in heavily salted water until tender. Drain and, while still warm, peel them. Pass the potatoes through a potato ricer onto a clean work surface. Spread the potato crumbles to allow steam to escape; moisture is the enemy of light gnocchi. Once cooled slightly, sprinkle flour and salt over the potatoes. Make a well in the center, add the beaten egg and nutmeg, and gently fold the ingredients together. Knead minimally just until a dough forms. Roll the dough into long ropes, cut into 1-inch pillows, and press them with a fork if desired. Set aside on a floured tray. 2. Sear the Scallops: Season the dried scallops with salt only moments before cooking. Heat oil in a stainless steel or cast-iron skillet over high heat until shimmering. Place scallops in the pan, ensuring they do not touch. Sear undisturbed for 2 minutes until a golden-brown crust forms. Flip, add 1 tablespoon of butter to the pan, baste for 30 seconds, and immediately remove them to a warm plate. 3. The Lemon-Butter Sauce: In a wide sauté pan, sauté the minced shallot in a tiny knob of butter over medium heat until translucent. Deglaze the pan with the white wine, scraping up any browned bits. Reduce the liquid by half. Lower the heat to the minimum and whisk in the chilled butter, one cube at a time, to create a stable emulsion. Stir in the lemon juice and zest. 4. Assembly: Boil the gnocchi in salted water. As soon as they float to the surface, they are ready. Use a slotted spoon to transfer them directly into the lemon-butter sauce. Add a splash of pasta water and toss gently to coat. To plate, divide the gnocchi between two warmed shallow bowls.

title: German music in a 'zombie' state
text: For decades, Germany has been celebrated as the heartbeat of European classical music, a nation where the legacies of Bach, Beethoven, and Brahms are treated with a reverence bordering on the religious. However, a growing chorus of critics, musicians, and cultural analysts is warning that the country’s musical landscape is entering a "zombie" state—technically alive and performing, but lacking the vital soul, innovation, and economic dynamism required to thrive in the 21st century. The term, increasingly used in academic and journalistic circles, describes a phenomenon where Germany’s musical institutions—its grand opera houses, state-funded orchestras, and conservatories—continue to function through sheer momentum and heavy subsidies, yet fail to engage with the contemporary world. They are performing the "hits" of the past with flawless precision, but they are no longer creating the future. "We are seeing a perfection of the museum," says Elena Richter, a Berlin-based musicologist. "The technical standards of German orchestras are arguably the highest in the world. But there is a sense of stagnation. We are playing the same repertoire, in the same halls, for the same demographic, while the rest of the world is moving toward hybrid genres, digital integration, and diverse storytelling." At the heart of this crisis is a systemic reliance on the state subsidy model. Germany boasts one of the highest densities of cultural funding in the world, which has historically protected artists from the volatility of the market. While this has preserved high art, critics argue it has also created a "comfort trap." Without the pressure to innovate or the need to compete for a global audience, many institutions have become inward-looking, prioritizing tradition over evolution. This insulation has led to a widening generational gap. While younger audiences are gravitating towards electronic music, hip-hop, and genre-bending experimentalism, the traditional bastions of high culture are struggling to remain relevant. The "zombie" state is characterized by this disconnect: a high-functioning infrastructure that serves a shrinking, aging audience, while the creative energy of the youth migrates toward unregulated, independent spaces. Furthermore, the lack of diversity is being cited as a primary reason for this cultural paralysis. The canon remains overwhelmingly white and male, and the institutional structures governing music education and orchestral hiring are slow to reflect the multicultural reality of modern Germany. "A culture that does not reflect its people is a culture that is merely haunting its own history," says Marcus Weber, a conductor of the new wave. "If we only look backward, we are just ghosts performing for ghosts." Economic pressures are also beginning to bite. As municipal budgets tighten across the country, the era of unconditional support is coming to an end. Institutions that have spent decades ignoring digital transformation and audience engagement are finding themselves ill-equipped to navigate a leaner fiscal environment. The challenge for Germany is not to abandon its glorious heritage, but to reanimate it. To move beyond the zombie state, the nation’s musical institutions must find a way to marry their unparalleled technical excellence with a spirit of risk-taking.

title: Display Handicap
text: In sports and competitive gaming, a display handicap refers to the visual representation of a player's skill level, performance history, or a mathematical adjustment applied to their score to facilitate fair competition. Unlike a physical handicap, such as a weighted ball in bowling, a display handicap is a data-driven metric used to normalize the playing field between participants of unequal ability. It is primarily used in systems where players compete against a standard or against one another under adjusted scoring conditions. Mathematical Basis and Function The core purpose of a display handicap is to provide a transparent view of a player's relative standing. In many competitive environments, this is calculated using a moving average of past performances. For example, in golf, the handicap index is a numerical value that represents a player's potential ability. When this value is "displayed" alongside a player's name on a leaderboard, it allows spectators and competitors to understand that a player shooting a 90 may actually be performing better relative to their skill level than a player shooting an 80. In many digital environments, the display handicap serves as a matchmaking tool. In competitive video games (esports), the "hidden" Elo or MMR (Matchmaking Rating) is often translated into a visible display handicap, such as a tier (Gold, Platinum, Diamond) or a numerical rank. This display serves as a psychological and social marker of progress, while the underlying mathematics ensure that players are paired with opponents of similar skill. Applications in Various Fields Golf and Traditional Sports In golf, the display handicap is an integral part of the game's etiquette and competitive structure. Tournament leaderboards often feature a column for the handicap to provide context to the gross score. This allows for the calculation of a "net score," which is the actual score used to determine the winner in handicap competitions. Without the display of this metric, the nuance of skill-based competition would be lost to casual observers. Esports and Online Gaming In the realm of online multiplayer gaming, display handicaps are used to manage player expectations and maintain competitive integrity. Because modern matchmaking systems are highly complex, developers often implement a "visible rank" to act as a simplified display handicap. This prevents the frustration of players feeling they are facing insurmountable odds by providing a clear, albeit simplified, indication of the skill gap between them and their opponents. Board Games and Skill-Based Competitions In games such as chess or various tabletop wargames, a display handicap may take the form of material advantages or temporal constraints. For instance, in a chess match between a Grandmaster and a novice, the handicap might be displayed as a "piece deficit" for the Grandmaster, visually indicating that the stronger player is starting at a disadvantage to ensure a competitive game. Psychological and Social Impact The display of a handicap has significant psychological implications. For high-level competitors, a displayed handicap can serve as a measure of prestige and social standing within a community.

text: Milosh Forman’s *Man on the Moon* is a film that exists in the volatile, beautiful, and often contradictory space between biography and character study. While many biopics fall into the trap of a chronological, "birth-to-death" assembly line, Forman opts for something far more rhythmic and chaotic, mirroring the very subject it seeks to capture: Andy Kaufman. It is a film that refuses to provide a definitive answer to the question of who Kaufman actually was, and in doing so, it achieves a level of truth that a more traditional documentary-style approach never could. Jim Carrey delivers what is arguably the most disciplined and transformative performance of his career. For much of his filmography, Carrey’s brilliance lies in his kinetic, rubber-faced elasticity—a superhuman ability to manipulate his features for immediate comedic payoff. Here, he tempers that energy, channeling it into a much more unsettling, internalised performance. He captures Kaufman’s profound loneliness and his pathological need to blur the lines between performance and reality. Carrey doesn't just "play" Andy; he inhabits the specific, manic frequency that Andy operated on. There is a vulnerability in Carrey’s eyes during the quieter moments with Lynne Loxton (Lauren Holly) that provides the emotional anchor necessary to keep the film from drifting into pure eccentricity. The film’s structure is intentionally disjointed, leaping between various eras of Kaufman’s career and his personal relationship with Loxton. This non-linear approach serves a purpose: it mimics the experience of watching Kaufman himself. To watch a Kaufman performance was to be unsure if you were witnessing a joke, a prank, or a genuine breakdown. By fragmenting the narrative, Forman forces the audience into that same state of uncertainty. We are never quite sure when the "character" ends and the "man" begins, which is perhaps the most honest way to portray a figure whose entire existence was predicated on the subversion of identity. The supporting cast is equally stellar, with several actors playing heightened, almost caricatured versions of real-life figures, which adds to the surrealist atmosphere. The film captures the specific, gritty energy of the late 70s and early 80s comedy scene, but it avoids being a mere nostalgia trip. Instead, it uses that setting to explore the isolation of the artist. Kaufman is presented as a man who viewed the world as a stage, but once the curtain fell, he found himself in a vacuum of his own making. If there is a criticism to be leveled, it is that the film occasionally struggles to find its tonal center. The shift from the high-concept absurdity of his comedy sketches to the tender, heartbreaking developments of his personal life can feel jarring. However, one could argue that this tonal whiplash is the point. Life, much like Kaufman’s art, is rarely a smooth transition from laughter to grief. Ultimately, *Man on the Moon* is not just a movie about a comedian; it is a meditation on the masks we wear and the heavy cost of constant performance.

title: Julia Child'S Duck A L'Orange
text: Julia Child's Duck à l'Orange Duck à l'Orange is the great classic of French cooking, and there is nothing quite so wonderful as a well-roasted duck with a glossy, bittersweet orange sauce. Do not be intimidated—take your time, and remember that a sauce can always be corrected. Bon appétit! Ingredients One duck, 4½ to 5 pounds, with neck and giblets reserved Salt and freshly ground black pepper 3 large oranges 1 carrot, sliced 1 onion, sliced 1 tablespoon sugar 3 tablespoons red wine vinegar 2 cups chicken stock (or duck stock, if you have it) 1½ tablespoons cornstarch or arrowroot 2 tablespoons unsalted butter 2 tablespoons orange liqueur (optional but delightful) Serves 4 to 6 Instructions Roasting the duck: Preheat your oven to 375°F. Remove the giblets and save the liver for another use. Cut off the wing tips and excess fat from the duck's cavity. Truss the duck so it will roast evenly. Then—and this is essential—prick the skin all over with a sharp fork, especially around the thighs and breast. You are piercing only the fat layer, not the meat. Season the cavity and skin generously with salt and pepper. Place the duck breast-up on a rack in your roasting pan. Roast for about 1½ hours, pouring off the accumulated fat every 20 minutes or so. Do save this fat—it is liquid gold for frying potatoes! The duck is done when the skin is a handsome brown and the legs move easily in their sockets. Remove the duck to a platter and keep it warm while you make the sauce. The orange preparation: While the duck roasts, remove strips of zest from two oranges with a vegetable peeler, avoiding the bitter white pith. Cut the zest into fine juliennes and blanch them in boiling water for 5 minutes; drain and set aside. Squeeze the juice from two oranges—you will need about ½ cup. Peel the third orange, removing all pith, and cut the flesh into neat segments. Set these aside for garnish. The sauce: Pour the fat out of your roasting pan, add the sliced carrot and onion, and brown them lightly on the stove. Deglaze with a bit of stock, scraping up all those delicious browned juices—this is flavor! Strain the liquid into a saucepan and add the rest of the stock, simmering to reduce slightly. Now make your caramel: In a small saucepan, boil the sugar with the vinegar until it turns a deep syrupy brown and smells slightly of caramel. Pour in the orange juice—it will sputter furiously, so take care—then stir the mixture into your sauce. Blend the cornstarch with a few tablespoons of cold water and whisk it into the sauce. Simmer a minute or two until it thickens enough to coat a spoon lightly. Off the heat, swirl in the butter, then the liqueur if you are using it. Add the blanched zest and taste, taste, taste! Correct the seasoning. It should be a happy balance of sweet, bitter, and tart.

title: South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut
text: I first saw this movie in a theater the summer it came out, and I've been telling people ever since that it's one of the most underrated pieces of satire of the 1990s. Yes, it's crude. Yes, it's obscene. Yes, it probably has more curse words per minute than anything else ever committed to film. But it's also — and I say this without a hint of irony — a genuinely clever musical and one of the sharpest takedowns of censorship and moral panic ever made. The premise is so simple it's brilliant: the boys sneak into the R-rated Terrance and Phillip movie, walk out spouting an exciting new vocabulary, and their parents respond by declaring war on Canada. That escalation — from a dirty movie to an actual war, complete with scheduled executions — sounds absurd, and it is, but that's the point. Parker and Stone understand that moral panic IS absurd. Every adult in the movie reacts to their children's behavior by blaming someone else, and the whole plot is built on that deflection. The parents blame Canada, the government blames Terrance and Phillip, and everybody scrambles to avoid the terrifying possibility of looking in a mirror. "Blame Canada" is hilarious on the surface, but the lyrics — "we must blame them and cause a fuss before somebody thinks of blaming us" — are a more honest summary of American political life than most serious films manage. And the songs! I wasn't prepared for how good the music is. "Uncle F*a" is filthy in exactly the way a Broadway parody should be, but "It's Easy, Mmmkay" is a legitimately well-constructed number with rhymes that would make Sondheim smirk. "Up There," Satan's big ballad, is played completely straight — a yearning "I Want" song straight out of a Disney film — and it works because Parker and Stone genuinely know the conventions they're sending up. "Blame Canada" getting an Oscar nomination was the cherry on top: the Academy honoring a song whose entire thesis is scapegoating, with nobody catching the irony. The subplot with Satan and Saddam Hussein still kills me. Satan as a lonely, sensitive soul trapped in an abusive relationship with Saddam shouldn't work, but the sincerity makes it weirdly touching, and it feeds into an ending that gives Kenny — the character who dies constantly — an actual emotional payoff. I never expected a South Park movie to make me feel something, and there I was in the theater, a little moved. Ridiculous, but true. What impresses me most on rewatch is how tight it is. Barely eighty minutes, no fat, every joke and musical number serving the story. The animation is deliberately cheap, but the writing is anything but — gags come so fast and from so many directions (the V-chip, the MPAA jabs, the finale that's somehow both sincere and mocking) that the movie stays a step ahead of you the whole way.

text: January 1. The old year died as I will die: in sleep, not knowing when the white came down on it. I wake to a world cancelled and made clean as any soul that God has walked through fire. I am the fire, Lord; walk me through myself. January 3. They say you answer prayer. I have prayed long and heard no voice, yet something kept me praying— a hunger that was half a memory of bread. Perhaps the hunger is the answer. Perhaps the aching is your hand against my wall. January 6. Epiphany. The magi kneel again in every painted window, gold in hand. I have no gold. I bring you my cold fear, my January of the heart. Take that. It cost me more than frankincense and myrrh. January 9. The young ask what age is like. I do not say it is a country where the friends have thinned, where every stair is taller than before. I say it is a room grown quiet, God, until a man must listen or go mad. January 12. I dreamed last night the house in which I was a boy was snowed to the chimneys. At the window, my father stood looking up. No one was in the room but me. I could have wept, waking. Or knelt. The dead are not far off who lived so near. January 15. Midwinter now, midpoint of the long gray. Even my doubts are tired of being doubted. Old sins come visiting like country cousins who do not know when it is time to leave. Lord, you must be the host who shows them out. January 18. I quarreled with you this morning at the sink, both hands in water warm as any mercy. I said: If you are love, why all this dark? The tap ran on. The cup came clean. No thunder. Only, some way, my anger washed away. January 21. A thaw. The eaves let go their silver teeth. Under the white the grass is grudging green. So, soul, take heart: beneath the frozen wrong something of you remembers being spring, and waits there, small as seed, against the light. January 24. A bird this morning—one—sang three notes, and stopped, as if ashamed of being heard so soon. Sing on, small friend. Winter is real, but so are you. I will believe for both of us until my own thawed throat remembers how. January 27. My hands upon my knees, the old dog breathing, the fire ticking like an unhurried clock. I am not frightened at the dark, but curious. I think death is a door held open wide by someone who has waited there all along. January 30. They say the old grow near to heaven. Some days I feel only nearer to my own grave earth. But you, if you are anywhere, are there in the gap between the two, and know my name before I call it out across the cold. January 31.

text: Dear Editor, I am writing to add my voice to the debate about computers and their effect on our daily lives. Some of your readers seem to believe that these machines are pulling us away from exercise, nature, and one another. I understand that worry, but I firmly believe that computers, when used sensibly, do far more good than harm—and I would like to persuade your readers to see them as the remarkable tools they are. Consider first what a computer puts within reach of every family in this town. A child can explore the Great Barrier Reef or the ruins of ancient Rome without buying a plane ticket. A student struggling with algebra can find patient, clear explanations at any hour. When my classmates and I researched our local history project, we uncovered photographs and newspaper archives that would otherwise have sat untouched in a library basement. My own grandmother, who lives three hundred miles away, now watches my little brother's birthday parties through video calls and no longer feels cut off from our lives. Distance used to separate families; now it need only separate their bodies, not their hearts. Add to this the practical skills—typing, research, hand-eye coordination from interactive games—that employers increasingly expect, and it becomes clear that the computer is not a luxury but a doorway. Some argue that time spent at a screen is time stolen from fresh air and friendship. But surely the fault lies with our choices, not with the machine. A hammer can build a bookshelf or smash a window; no one blames the hammer. If a person sits indoors all weekend, the solution is not to ban computers but to build better habits around them. Indeed, the same computer that tempts us to stay inside can send us out: my family has used ours to find hiking trails we never knew existed, to check the weather before a picnic, and to learn which birds visit our feeder each spring. The technology did not replace our walk in the park; it improved it. The same is true of family life. Critics claim computers silence the dinner table, and in homes without rules that can happen. Yet in my house, the computer has sparked more conversations than it has ended: we share funny videos, plan holidays together, and my parents use it to help me with homework they long ago forgot how to do. Screens are only antisocial when we let them be. A family that agrees on sensible limits—an hour after homework, none at the dinner table—soon discovers that the computer, like the television before it, can be a companion to family life rather than its rival. Of course, I am not asking anyone to live online. Exercise, sunlight, and face-to-face friendship are as necessary as food, and no sensible person should sacrifice them.

Add the ground beef, ground pork, grated onion, beaten egg, all‑spice, white pepper, nutmeg, and ½ tsp salt. Mix gently with your hands or a fork until just combined—over‑mixing makes the meatballs dense. 2. title: Hurricane Esther
text: Hurricane Esther was a long‑lived and erratic Cape Verde‑type tropical cyclone that affected the Atlantic basin during the 1961 hurricane season. Originating from a tropical wave off the coast of West Africa on September 3, Esther attained Category 5 intensity on the Saffir–Simpson scale, maintaining peak winds of 165 mph (265 km h⁻¹) for 24 hours—the longest duration at that intensity on record at the time. Though the storm ultimately brushed the eastern seaboard of the United States, its most significant impacts were felt at sea and in the Caribbean, where it produced catastrophic wind damage, extensive flooding, and a high number of maritime casualties. Meteorological history A tropical wave emerged from the African continent on September 2, 1961 and quickly organized into a tropical depression east of the Cape Verde Islands by 12:00 UTC on September 3. The system was designated Tropical Storm Esther six hours later as reconnaissance aircraft recorded sustained winds of 45 mph (75 km h⁻¹). Favorable environmental conditions—low vertical wind shear, sea‑surface temperatures exceeding 28 °C (82 °F), and robust upper‑level outflow—promoted rapid intensification. By September 5 Esther had reached hurricane strength and, on September 6, was classified as a major hurricane (Category 3). From September 7 to 9 the cyclone underwent an explosive deepening phase, with its central pressure falling from 980 mbar to 921 mbar, while maximum sustained winds surged to 165 mph, making Esther a Category 5 hurricane. The storm tracked west‑northwestward across the central Atlantic, executing a large clockwise loop between 32° N and 45° W, an unusual motion attributed to the interaction with a strengthening subtropical ridge to its north. After peaking, Esther gradually weakened as it encountered increasing wind shear and cooler waters near the western edge of the Gulf Stream. By September 13 the hurricane had downgraded to Category 2 and began an erratic northeastward drift, executing several small loops that extended its lifespan to a record 23 days as a tropical system. The cyclone turned toward the United States on September 15, passing just east of the Outer Banks, North Carolina, with wind gusts of 80 mph (130 km h⁻¹) in coastal communities. On September 18 Esther merged with an extratropical low over the North Atlantic, completing its transition to a powerful extratropical cyclone that later impacted Iceland with gale‑force winds. Preparations Forecasts issued by the United States Weather Bureau and the U.S. Navy’s Joint Typhoon Warning Center highlighted the potential for a direct landfall on the East Coast. In North Carolina, over 200,000 residents were ordered to evacuate coastal barrier islands, and emergency shelters were opened in nine counties. The U.S. Coast Guard pre‑positioned 12 cutters along the Atlantic seaboard, and the Navy placed aircraft carriers on standby. Caribbean nations—including the Bahamas, Bermuda, and the Lesser Antilles—issued tropical storm warnings, with the Bahamas evacuating tourists from offshore resorts. Impact Atlantic Ocean: Esther’s most severe effects occurred at sea.

text: Hitchcock’s “Saboteur” is a lean, high‑octane wartime thriller that feels both grounded in the era’s anxieties and surprisingly timeless in its execution. The premise is simple but effective: an innocent man, a canny architect named Barry Kane (Robert Montgomery), is framed for a murder he didn’t commit and forced on the run, all while a shadowy enemy organization plots sabotage on American soil. From the opening beat, the film spins a web of paranoia that keeps the audience’s attention, and Hitchcock’s deft hand ensures that the tension never flags, even as the narrative barrels toward its climactic showdown on the Statue of Liberty. Montgomery delivers a solid performance as the every‑man hero thrust into extraordinary circumstances. He balances vulnerability with a quiet determination that makes his plight feel authentic rather than merely plot‑driven. The chemistry between Montgomery and Priscilla Lane, who plays his resourceful girlfriend Pat, is understated but effective; Lane’s Pat is far more than a damsel in distress—she’s proactive, quick‑thinking, and willing to jump into danger alongside Barry. Their partnership fuels much of the film’s emotional core, and their occasional banter provides brief, welcome breathers amid the relentless chase. The supporting cast shines in their respective roles. Alan Hale Sr., as the grizzled trucker who helps the duo evade capture, delivers a rugged charm that heightens the film’s sense of a ragtag resistance forming against a faceless enemy. The antagonists, particularly the cold‑blooded Karl (Walt Anderson) and the menacing "Pete" (Albert Dekker), are suitably menacing without descending into caricature, a balance that many wartime movies of the era struggle to achieve. Hitchcock also employs memorable cameos—most notably a brief appearance by a nervous telegraph operator delivering a critical clue—that add texture to the world he builds. Stylistically, “Saboteur” showcases Hitchcock’s signature command of suspense and visual storytelling. The title sequence, a simple black‑and‑white opening with stark, angular type, sets a foreboding tone that carries through the film’s chiaroscuro lighting and stark compositions. The chase sequences are particularly noteworthy; the motor‑truck pursuit across the desert and the frantic subway chase use rapid cuts and tight framing to convey urgency without relying on elaborate special effects. The climactic face‑off atop the Statue of Liberty is both a literal and metaphorical summit, framing the conflict against an iconic American symbol that underscores the film’s war‑time propaganda undertones while also providing a breathtaking visual payoff. The screenplay, written by Alan Le May and Martin Rackin, balances exposition with action. Hitchcock senses the need to explain the saboteur network’s motives without bogging the narrative down, and he accomplishes this through concise dialogue and effective visual cues. The pacing is brisk; at just under ninety minutes, the film never lingers, and each scene propels the story forward. That efficiency, however, sometimes sacrifices deeper character development—Barry’s backstory remains largely unexplored, and the enemy organization feels more an abstraction than a fully realized threat. text: I am using a 40 MHz surface‑mount crystal (Epson XRCGB40M000F1S1BR0) in a custom PCB that drives a simple oscillator circuit. According to the crystal’s datasheet the load capacitance is 12 pF (typical), and the oscillator should therefore run at its fundamental frequency of 40 MHz. When I power the board and probe the output with an oscilloscope (10× probe, 100 MHz bandwidth) I see a clean, sinusoidal waveform at 96 MHz, not at 40 MHz. The amplitude is about 2 Vpp, and the waveform is stable over temperature and supply variations. If I switch the oscillator into “test mode” by pulling the TEST pin of the inverter high (as described in the device’s application note), the output frequency drops to the expected 40 MHz, though the signal is slightly noisier. In normal operation (TEST pin low) the 96 MHz signal is present and the circuit otherwise behaves as intended. I have double‑checked a few things: 1. Component values – The two load capacitors are indeed 33 pF (±5 %). I tried replacing them with 22 pF and 47 pF parts; the 96 MHz output persists, only the amplitude changes a little. 2. Crystal orientation – I swapped the crystal with a second, identical part from a different batch; the same behaviour occurs. 3. Supply voltage – The circuit runs from 3.3 V. Raising the supply to 5 V (within the inverter’s limits) does not affect the frequency. 4. Probe loading – Using a 1× probe (higher capacitance) still shows the 96 MHz signal, albeit with a slightly reduced amplitude. 5. Oscillator topology – I built a second board using a Schmitt‑trigger inverter (74LVC1G08) in place of the previous gate; the result is unchanged. 6. Measurement verification – I cross‑checked the frequency with a spectrum analyzer (0–3 GHz) and a frequency counter; both confirm ~96.0 MHz with <0.1 % variation. The crystal’s datasheet mentions a “normal mode” and a “test mode”. In normal mode the crystal is intended to be used as a reference for a PLL, while in test mode the crystal is driven directly at its fundamental frequency. However, the datasheet does not explain why the normal‑mode configuration would cause the crystal to oscillate at almost exactly 2.4 × its nominal frequency. My current hypotheses are: Harmonic oscillation – Perhaps the inverter’s gain and phase shift at higher frequencies allow the circuit to lock onto a harmonic (the third harmonic would be 120 MHz, the second 80 MHz, but 96 MHz is close to 2.4 ×40 MHz, which does not correspond to a simple integer harmonic). Could a spurious mode of the crystal be excited? Mode switching within the crystal – Some crystals have a spurious “overtone” mode; maybe the XRCGB40M000F1S1BR0 has a designed overtone near 96 MHz that is being unintentionally selected.

The Canon is meant to secure reliable knowledge about the world without appealing to any metaphysical speculation. Yet Epicurus famously posits a materialist physics of atoms moving in the void, a doctrine that seems to go well beyond what can be directly sensed. This raises a puzzling question for me: how does Epicurus’s own epistemic framework actually justify belief in atoms and void, given that these entities are, by definition, invisible and unobservable? Moreover, is the mere “non‑contestation” of a hypothesis—i.e., the lack of any apparent reason to doubt it—sufficient grounds for accepting it as true within Epicurean thought? My confusion stems from three interlocking issues: 1. The status of the Canon’s criteria. Epicurus writes that knowledge is based on what is directly perceived (the “canon of sensations”) and on what can be correctly anticipated from those perceptions (the “canon of anticipations”). He also allows that “the absence of a contrary impression” (*atheoria*) can support a claim. However, he does not appear to treat a priori reasoning or inference from unseen causes as a primary source of knowledge. If the Canon is limited to what is directly present to the senses, how can it accommodate a theory like atomism, where the fundamental constituents of reality are forever beyond sensory access? 2. The role of anticipations and analogical inference. Some commentators (e.g., Lucretius in *De Rerum Natura*, 1‑2) argue that Epicurus employed analogical reasoning: we perceive the motion of tangible bodies and infer that similar motions must be produced by smaller, indivisible particles. Yet Epicurus himself seems to reserve anticipations for “regularly recurring phenomena” (e.g., the expectation that fire will be hot). Are anticipations strong enough to bridge the gap between observable macroscopic events and the invisible micro‑world? If so, what justificatory force does this give to atomistic claims, and does it differ from mere conjecture? 3. The “non‑contestation” clause. Epicurus famously asserts that “nothing is more wonderful than that which is certain, and the surest thing is that which is not contested” (Letter to Menoeceus, 47). Some scholars (e.g., Irwin, *The Development of Ethics* 1999) interpret this as an endorsement of a kind of “pragmatic minimalism”: if there is no empirical reason to doubt a hypothesis, we may accept it provisionally. Does this mean that, for Epicurus, atomism is justified simply because no sensory evidence directly contradicts it, and because it offers explanatory power? Or does the Canon require a stronger, positive confirmatory basis—such as a perceptible effect that can only be explained by the existence of atoms and void? In attempting to answer these questions, I have considered the following possibilities, none of which seem wholly satisfactory: Indirect observation: Perhaps Epicurus counts the predictable behavior of falling bodies, the brittleness of certain substances, etc., as indirect “sensations” of atomic interactions.

text: Sir Keir Starmer has long struggled with the charge that his party lacks definition, that it is a vessel waiting to be filled with meaning only after polling day. On Tuesday, in a carefully choreographed moment at a mattress factory in the Midlands, the Labour leader attempted to answer that criticism with brevity rather than volume. "Country first, party second." The four words, emblazoned on a new campaign podium and repeated twelve times during his thirty-seven minute address, represent the most concentrated expression of Starmer's pitch to the British electorate. They are, his advisers hope, sufficiently capacious to accommodate voters of divergent political instincts while offering a clear tonal break from the Johnson and Sunak era. The formulation carries deliberate echoes of Gordon Brown's "No time for a novice" and even Tony Blair's "New Labour, New Britain," though Starmer's version notably omits his party's name entirely. That absence is telling. Labour strategists have pored over focus group data suggesting that the party brand remains toxic to a significant minority of voters who backed the Conservatives in 2019 but have since grown disillusioned. The slogan is designed to function as a political Trojan horse. "These four words are doing considerable work," says Professor Meg Russell, director of the Constitution Unit at University College London. "They invoke a tradition of patriotic service that Labour has sometimes struggled to claim, while implicitly criticising the Conservative party for putting its own survival—its permutations of leadership, its factional disputes—ahead of the national interest. It's simultaneously an offering and an attack." The immediate Conservative response sought to puncture this framing. Chancellor Jeremy Hunt, campaigning in Surrey, noted that Starmer had served in Jeremy Corbyn's shadow cabinet and "voted to make that man prime minister." The rebuttal, delivered with evident relish, illustrates the bind Starmer faces: any claim to have transcended party must contend with a recent past that opponents can readily invoke. Yet the four words also address a more immediate strategic imperative. With Reform UK consistently polling above fifteen per cent and the Liberal Democrats advancing in the south, Labour cannot rely on a purely negative anti-Conservative message. Starmer needs to harvest votes from multiple sources simultaneously, and the studied vagueness of his slogan is arguably a feature rather than a bug. At the factory in Daventry, where workers in high-vis jackets formed a politely attentive backdrop, Starmer deployed the phrase in contexts both expected and otherwise. It preceded commitments to defence spending and to the NHS, to stricter immigration controls and to green energy investment. Each policy, however contradictory it might appear to rigorous analysis, was subordinated to the overarching pledge of national prioritisation. Whether this rhetorical architecture can withstand scrutiny is another matter. title: Dairy-Free Amaretto-Fudge Gelato
text: Dairy-Free Amaretto-Fudge Gelato For the Gelato Base: 2 cans (13.5 oz each) full-fat coconut milk ½ cup raw cashews, soaked in water for 4 hours and drained ¾ cup granulated sugar ¼ cup light corn syrup 2 tablespoons cornstarch ¼ teaspoon fine sea salt 1 teaspoon vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract 3 tablespoons amaretto liqueur For the Fudge Ripple: 4 ounces bittersweet chocolate (70% cacao), finely chopped ½ cup full-fat coconut cream (scooped from top of chilled coconut milk can) 2 tablespoons amaretto liqueur 1 tablespoon light corn syrup Pinch of fine sea salt Begin by preparing your gelato base. Combine the soaked cashews and one can of coconut milk in a high-speed blender. Process on high for 2 to 3 minutes until completely smooth and creamy, with no visible cashew pieces remaining. This step is crucial for achieving the silky texture that mimics traditional dairy gelato, as the cashews provide richness and body that might otherwise come from egg yolks or heavy cream. In a medium saucepan, whisk together the sugar, cornstarch, and salt. Gradually whisk in the remaining can of coconut milk until no lumps remain. Set the saucepan over medium heat and cook, stirring constantly with a heatproof spatula, until the mixture begins to steam and eventually thickens slightly, about 8 to 10 minutes. You are looking for a consistency that coats the back of a spoon and leaves a clean line when you run your finger through it. Remove the saucepan from heat and whisk in the cashew mixture, followed by the vanilla and amaretto. The amaretto not only contributes its distinctive almond flavor but also helps lower the freezing point, resulting in a softer, more scoopable gelato. Strain the base through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl to ensure absolute smoothness. Cover the surface directly with plastic wrap to prevent a skin from forming, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours or preferably overnight. The base must be thoroughly chilled before churning to achieve proper aeration and texture. While the base chills, prepare the fudge ripple. Place the chopped chocolate in a heatproof bowl. In a small saucepan, combine the coconut cream, amaretto, corn syrup, and salt. Bring to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally. Pour the hot cream mixture over the chocolate and let stand for 2 minutes without stirring. Then whisk until glossy and completely smooth. Let cool to room temperature, then transfer to a squeeze bottle or piping bag for easy drizzling. The fudge should be fluid but not runny when incorporated into the gelato. When your base is thoroughly chilled, churn in an ice cream maker according to the manufacturer's instructions, typically 25 to 35 minutes. The gelato is ready when it has increased in volume and resembles soft-serve, holding its shape but still malleable. Working quickly, spread one-third of the churned gelato into a freezer-safe container. Drizzle one-third of the fudge ripple over the surface, then use a knife or skewer to create decorative swirls.

text: The morning light costs nothing, slipping through the crack in curtains frayed to cobweb lace, and I have learned to wear my hours loose, unbuttoned at the collar, free of chase. title: The Ultimate Barbecued Ribs
text: The Ultimate Barbecued Ribs Select two full racks of Saint Louis–style pork ribs, each weighing approximately two and a half to three pounds. The meat should display even marbling with a rosy pink color, and the membrane on the bone side must be intact for proper removal. Begin eight to twenty-four hours before cooking by preparing the dry rub. Combine one-third cup dark brown sugar, two tablespoons smoked paprika, one tablespoon kosher salt, one tablespoon freshly cracked black pepper, one tablespoon garlic powder, one tablespoon onion powder, two teaspoons mustard powder, two teaspoons ground cumin, one teaspoon cayenne pepper, and one teaspoon celery seed. Whisk thoroughly to eliminate clumps. Remove the membrane by sliding a butter knife beneath the silver skin covering the bone side of each rack. Loosen enough to grip with a paper towel, then peel away in one firm motion. Pat the ribs completely dry with additional paper towels. Apply the dry rub generously across both surfaces, massaging into every crevice. Wrap each rack tightly in plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least eight hours, allowing the salt to penetrate deeply and the spices to anchor themselves to the meat. Three hours before dinner, remove the ribs from refrigeration and unwrap them. Fire your charcoal grill using the two-zone method, banking all coals to one side. Add three fist-sized chunks of hickory or oak to the hot coals. Stabilize the temperature at 225 degrees Fahrenheit on the cool side, verified with a probe thermometer clipped to the grate. Place an aluminum drip pan filled with one cup apple juice beneath where the ribs will rest. Position the racks bone-side down on the cool zone, running parallel to the flame with slight curvature to promote even smoke circulation. Close the lid with vents positioned to draw smoke across the meat before escaping. Maintain temperature between 225 and 250 degrees for the duration. After two hours, the exterior should have developed a deep mahogany bark. Remove the ribs and lay each rack on a large sheet of heavy-duty aluminum foil. Drizzle one-quarter cup honey along the top of each, followed by two tablespoons unsalted butter cut into small pieces. Tightly crimp the foil to seal completely, then return to the grill, still bone-side down, for ninety minutes. This step gently braises the connective tissue, rendering fat and transforming collagen into succulent gelatin. Combine the barbecue sauce while waiting. Simmer one and one-half cups ketchup, one-third cup molasses, one-third cup apple cider vinegar, one-quarter cup dark brown sugar, two tablespoons Worcestershire sauce, two tablespoons yellow mustard, one tablespoon liquid smoke, one teaspoon black pepper, and one-half teaspoon cayenne in a saucepan over medium heat. Reduce until thick enough to coat the back of a spoon, approximately fifteen minutes. Set aside one-third of this sauce for serving; the remainder will glaze the meat. The federation functions, she notes, as a machine for concentrating wealth in the capital while managing dissent through patronage networks and periodic violence. Her turning point arrives gradually. Chen's daughter disappears into detention for six weeks, emerging with permanent hearing damage from custody conditions. Chen resigns publicly, joins the separatist coordination committee, and helps draft the unilateral declaration that will lead to her imprisonment. title: When should visual synchronization be a requirement in a multi-browser automation system?
text: Our team is building a multi-browser automation system that executes test scenarios across Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge simultaneously. The core architecture uses a shared instruction dispatcher that broadcasts commands to all browser instances, with each instance maintaining its own WebDriver connection and state machine. We're debating whether visual synchronization—ensuring that screenshots or DOM representations match across browsers at specific checkpoints—should be a strict requirement or an optional layer. The primary use case is cross-browser compatibility testing for a SaaS platform with roughly 200 distinct user flows. Currently, we assert functional equivalence (same data persistence, API calls, event firing) but not visual equivalence. Some stakeholders argue that without visual synchronization, we might miss rendering differences that don't affect functionality but degrade user experience. Others contend that enforcing visual sync creates brittle tests and significant performance overhead. Our system currently handles timing variability through explicit waits and polling mechanisms, but browsers diverge in how quickly they execute JavaScript, render CSS, and complete layout passes. We've observed that Firefox often completes DOM updates 50-150ms slower than Chrome on complex interactions, while Safari's image decoding pipeline introduces different visual completion timing. These discrepancies don't affect functional outcomes but produce transient visual mismatches that would fail any naive screenshot comparison. We're considering three architectural approaches: (1) strict frame-level synchronization using a barrier mechanism that holds all browsers until each reports visual quiescence, (2) loose synchronization with configurable tolerance windows and perceptual diff thresholds, or (3) decoupling visual verification entirely into a separate pipeline that runs asynchronously and doesn't block test execution. The strict approach appeals from a theoretical correctness standpoint but introduces coordination complexity. We'd need a shared clock or logical ordering system, and we'd have to define "visual quiescence" precisely—which becomes problematic with infinite scroll, lazy-loaded images, CSS animations, and third-party widgets that may behave differently across browsers. We've prototyped this using MutationObserver combined with requestAnimationFrame callbacks, but the heuristic feels fragile and browser-specific. The loose approach seems pragmatic but raises questions about where to set thresholds. A 100ms tolerance might mask genuine bugs; a 500ms tolerance might make synchronization meaningless. Perceptual diff tools like Pixelmatch or proprietary solutions add their own configuration burden regarding anti-aliasing differences, subpixel rendering variations, and acceptable color deviation across browser rendering engines. Performance implications are substantial. Our test suite currently completes in 12 minutes when running functionally. Early experiments suggest strict visual synchronization extends this to 38-47 minutes, primarily due to waiting for the slowest browser at each synchronization point and the screenshot capture/comparison overhead. This threatens our goal of sub-20-minute feedback loops for developer commits. We're also uncertain about the signal-to-noise ratio. In our sample of 50 historical cross-browser bugs, 7 were purely visual (layout shifts, font rendering, missing shadows) without functional impact. However, 31 of those would not have been caught by DOM-level visual sync because they involved sub-pixel positioning, GPU compositing differences, or viewport-dependent breakpoints that our current responsive design handles through different code paths.

title: Solutions to the Cartesian Circle
text: I've been struggling with what seems to be a genuine problem in Descartes's epistemology, and I'm curious what responses have been offered to it. The worry is familiar enough: Descartes appears to argue that God's existence guarantees the truth of clear and distinct perceptions, yet his proof of God's existence itself relies on clear and distinct perceptions. This creates a circularity that threatens to undermine the entire edifice of his Meditations. Let me be more precise about what troubles me. In the Third Meditation, Descartes offers proofs for God's existence that depend on premises he claims to perceive clearly and distinctly—the causal principle, for instance, or the idea that the representative reality of an idea requires a cause with at least as much formal reality. Then in the Fifth Meditation and again in a more explicit way in the Second Replies, he seems to say that we need God's veracity to secure the general reliability of clear and distinct perceptions. If we need God to validate clear and distinct perceptions, but we need clear and distinct perceptions to prove God exists, we seem stuck in a circle. I've encountered several attempts to dissolve this problem, but none have fully satisfied me. One common strategy is what we might call the "memory interpretation," associated with commentators like Frankfurt. On this reading, Descartes only needs God's guarantee for the truth of past clear and distinct perceptions that we no longer attend to directly. When we actually perceive something clearly and distinctly, we cannot doubt it even in the hyperbolic scenario; the doubt only arises when we rely on memory. But I'm uncertain whether this fully escapes the circle. Even if the psychological certainty of current clear and distinct perceptions is indubitable, Descartes seems to want more than psychological certainty—he wants metaphysical guarantees that our faculties track truth. And doesn't the proof of God still require that we trust some clear and distinct perceptions as actually true, not merely as psychologically compelling? Another approach I've seen emphasizes the distinction between methodic doubt and ordinary epistemic practices. Perhaps Descartes is not trying to provide a foundational justification from scratch but rather showing how reason can vindicate itself when challenged. The circle, on this view, is not vicious because Descartes never really steps entirely outside his rational faculties—he's always operating within the space of reasons, showing how the deliverances of reason cohere. But I worry this makes Descartes into a kind of coherentist, which sits uncomfortably with his explicit foundationalist ambitions. I've also encountered the "cognitively self-evidencing" interpretation, where clear and distinct perceptions include within themselves an awareness of their own truth, and God's role is to explain why this internal mark reliably indicates truth rather than to add any further guarantee. Yet if clear and distinct perceptions are self-guaranteeing in this strong sense, what work is left for God to do? And doesn't this again risk making the theological machinery otiose?
