title: Warm Johnny Cakes With Blackberries
text: Warm Johnny Cakes With Blackberries Johnny cakes, also known as hoecakes, are a traditional Southern dish that's easy to make and incredibly comforting. Pairing them with fresh blackberries adds a burst of summer flavor that complements the hearty, slightly sweet cakes perfectly. This recipe serves 4 as a delightful breakfast or snack. Ingredients: For the Johnny Cakes: 1 cup yellow cornmeal 1/2 cup all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon baking powder 1/2 teaspoon salt 1/2 teaspoon baking soda 1 large egg 1 cup buttermilk 2 tablespoons unsalted butter, melted For the Blackberry Topping: 2 cups fresh blackberries 2 tablespoons granulated sugar 1 tablespoon lemon juice 1 tablespoon cornstarch mixed with 1 tablespoon water For Serving: 2 tablespoons butter, melted Powdered sugar, for dusting Maple syrup, optional Instructions: 1. Prepare the Johnny Cakes Batter: In a large bowl, combine the cornmeal, all-purpose flour, baking powder, salt, and baking soda. Whisk until well mixed. In a separate bowl, whisk together the egg, buttermilk, and melted butter. Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and stir until just combined. The batter should be slightly lumpy. Let the batter rest for about 10 minutes to allow the cornmeal to absorb some of the liquid. 2. Cook the Johnny Cakes: Heat a large skillet or griddle over medium heat and lightly grease it with a little bit of butter. For each johnny cake, pour about 1/4 cup of batter onto the skillet. Cook until bubbles form on the surface and the edges start to look set, about 3-4 minutes. Flip the cakes and cook for an additional 2-3 minutes, until golden brown and cooked through. Transfer the cooked johnny cakes to a plate and keep them warm while you cook the rest of the batter. 3. Make the Blackberry Topping: In a medium saucepan, combine the blackberries, sugar, and lemon juice. Cook over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the blackberries start to break down and release their juices, about 5 minutes. Stir in the cornstarch mixture and continue to cook until the mixture thickens, about 2-3 minutes. Remove from heat and set aside. 4. Warm the Johnny Cakes: Brush the warm johnny cakes with melted butter and dust them lightly with powdered sugar. 5. Serve: Place the johnny cakes on plates and spoon the blackberry topping over the top. You can also drizzle a bit of maple syrup over the top if desired. Enjoy them while they're warm! Tips: You can make the blackberry topping ahead of time and reheat it gently before serving. For an extra indulgent touch, serve the johnny cakes with a dollop of whipped cream or a side of yogurt. If you don't have buttermilk, you can substitute it with 1 cup of milk mixed with 1 tablespoon of lemon juice or vinegar, left to sit for 5 minutes. These Warm Johnny Cakes With Blackberries are sure to become a favorite in your household, offering a delightful blend of sweet, tart, and hearty flavors. Enjoy!

title: Why doesn't Hebrew have a distinct vocabulary for the divine realm?
text: In exploring the Hebrew language, particularly in the context of religious texts such as the Tanakh (Hebrew Bible), one notices a fascinating aspect: the lack of a distinct, dedicated vocabulary specifically for the divine realm. Unlike some other ancient and modern languages that have developed elaborate terms and phrases to describe the sacred and divine, Hebrew often uses the same words for mundane and divine contexts. This linguistic characteristic raises several intriguing questions about the nature of Hebrew and its theological implications. One of the most striking examples is the use of the word "שָׁמַיִם" (shamayim), which translates to "heavens." While shamayim is often used to refer to the divine realm or the abode of God, it also literally means "skies" or "heavens" in the physical sense. This dual usage suggests a profound connection between the material and spiritual worlds, reflecting a holistic view of creation where the divine is not separate from but interwoven with the natural world. Another example is the word "אֱלֹהִים" (Elohim), one of the primary names for God in the Hebrew Bible. Elohim is used not only to refer to the divine being but also, in certain contexts, to refer to judges or powerful human figures. This linguistic flexibility indicates that the concept of divinity is not isolated but rather encompasses a spectrum of authority and power that can be manifested in various forms, including human leadership. The Hebrew word "קרוב" (karov), meaning "near" or "close," is another intriguing example. It is used to describe both physical proximity and spiritual closeness to God. This duality underscores the idea that God is intimately involved in human life, bridges the gap between the earthly and heavenly realms, and emphasizes the importance of personal relationship and connection with the divine. The use of common terms for divine and mundane experiences aligns with the Jewish concept of immanence, where God is seen as closely tied to the world and human affairs. This stands in contrast to the notion of transcendence found in some other religious traditions, where the divine is often portrayed as distant and separate from the physical world. The immanent perspective encourages a more intimate and or even interdependent connection between humanity and the divine. Moreover, the Hebrew language often relies on metaphor and analogy to convey spiritual ideas. For instance, God is frequently described using human attributes and actions, such as seeing, hearing, and even experiencing emotions like love, anger, and regret. This anthropomorphic language serves to make the divine more relatable and comprehensible, reflecting the belief that God is not merely a distant deity but a personal and involved creator. The absence of a distinct divine vocabulary also has pedagogical implications. The use of everyday language to describe spiritual concepts encourages a deeper engagement with religious texts and teachings. It invites believers to reflect on the everyday experiences and realities that can serve as windows into the divine.

title: Safety architecture and black channel
text: In our current safety-critical control system, we are adhering strictly to IEC 61508 and ISO 26262 standards, aiming for ASIL D. The system architecture comprises two redundant microcontrollers (MCUs) operating in a lockstep or split-brain configuration, with an independent safety monitor MCU watching over them. This "safety island" is designed to detect faults and initiate a safe state if any anomaly is detected. However, we have encountered a significant design dilemma regarding the communication between the functional application logic and the safety monitor. Specifically, we are discussing the implementation of a "black channel" for certain critical data transfers. By "black channel," I am referring to a communication link that is not monitored for integrity, timing, or content by the safety monitor. The rationale from the functional side is that including these specific low-level status bits in the monitored data stream adds significant latency and jitter, which negatively impacts the real-time performance of the control loop. They argue that since this data is only used for diagnostic logging and non-critical UI updates, it does not influence the safe state determination and therefore does not require the overhead of CRC checks, timestamp verification, or heartbeat monitoring typically applied to "white" or "grey" channels. The safety case team is strongly opposed to this approach. They argue that any unmonitored communication path represents a potential entry point for a silent fault. If a bit flip occurs in this "black channel," it could theoretically propagate corruption to shared memory regions or, worse, influence the scheduling priorities of other tasks if the underlying driver code is not perfectly isolated. They contend that the "black" designation cannot be justified under ASIL D requirements because it breaks the chain of trust. In a strict safety architecture, every byte exchanged between the functional and safety domains should be verified. If it is not monitored, it cannot be claimed as safe, and thus the entire safety argument for the surrounding logic becomes tenuous. I am trying to find a middle ground or a theoretical basis to justify, or perhaps reject, the existence of this unmonitored channel. My primary concern is the definition of "safety-related" communication. If the data in question truly has zero influence on the actuator outputs or the state machine logic that governs the safe state, can it be classified as "non-safety-related" and thus excluded from the safety monitor’s scope? Or does the very act of sharing a physical bus or memory bus with safety-critical data make it inherently safety-related due to the risk of interference, such as bus contention or memory bank corruption? We have considered separating the hardware completely, using a different physical bus for this diagnostic data, but this is not feasible due to pin count limitations and cost constraints on the specific MCU series we are using. We also considered using a dedicated hardware FIFO that is accessible only to the functional MCU and a separate debug port, effectively removing it from the domain of the safety monitor entirely.

title: Schematic Review For A MAX7219 display with ESP32
text: I am building a project that requires driving four MAX7219 4-digit LED display modules using an ESP32. I have designed a schematic based on the typical daisy-chain configuration found in the MAX7219 datasheet and various online tutorials. My primary concern is signal integrity and potential power issues, as I am relatively new to interfacing with high-current display drivers. I would appreciate a review of the schematic to ensure I haven't overlooked any critical components or connections that could lead to device failure or erratic behavior. The system is powered by a 5V USB supply. I used a 1117-5.0 linear regulator to generate a stable 5V rail for the logic and the MAX7219 modules, as the ESP32 can tolerate up to 3.6V on its GPIO pins, but the MAX7219 requires 5V for proper driving capability of the LEDs. I placed a 10uF tantalum capacitor and a 100nF ceramic capacitor at the input of the regulator, and a 10uF and 100nF combination at the output, close to the pin 1 (V+) of each MAX7219 module. I believe this should handle the transient current spikes when the displays update, but I am unsure if 10uF is sufficient for a 4-module chain. Some sources suggest using larger bulk capacitors, perhaps 100uF, near the last module in the chain to handle the cumulative inductive kickback from the LED segments. Should I add these, or is my current placement adequate? Regarding the communication interface, I am using the standard 3-wire serial interface: DIN, CS, and CLK. I connected the CS line directly to GPIO 15 of the ESP32. Since the MAX7219 uses active-low chip select logic, I ensured the line is pulled high when not in use via an internal pull-up, though I also added a 10kΩ external pull-up resistor to VCC for stability. The DIN and CLK lines are connected to GPIO 16 and GPIO 17, respectively. I am aware that these GPIOs have internal pull-ups and pull-downs, but I have disabled them in the code to prevent any contention. I did not add series termination resistors to the signal lines, assuming the short length of the wires on my PCB (less than 5cm) would make them unnecessary. Is this a safe assumption at the 10MHz clock speed I plan to use? I have seen conflicting advice on whether series resistors (e.g., 33Ω) are needed to dampen ringing on the SPI lines, especially when multiple MAX7219s are daisy-chained. Another point of concern is the LED current limiting. The MAX7219 has a dedicated VLED pin that determines the segment current. I have connected this pin to VCC (5V) through a 0Ω resistor to allow maximum brightness, but I am reading that this might stress the device or cause excessive power consumption. I calculated that each digit consumes approximately 80mA when all segments are on, and with four modules, the total peak current could reach 1.28A plus the logic overhead.

text: To the Editor, The debate surrounding the impact of computers on our daily lives has become one of the most polarizing discussions of our time. On one hand, we are told that digital devices are the great equalizers, bridging geographical gaps and enhancing cognitive skills. On the other hand, critics argue that our screens are eroding our physical health, severing meaningful human connections, and disconnecting us from the natural world. While I acknowledge the profound risks associated with excessive screen time, I firmly believe that when used with intention and balance, computers serve as indispensable tools that enrich our lives, foster global empathy, and provide economic and educational opportunities that were previously unimaginable. We must not throw out the digital baby with the bathwater; instead, we must champion a healthier, more conscious relationship with technology. First, consider the unprecedented access to knowledge and education that computers provide. In the past, learning was often limited by geography, economic status, or the availability of local institutions. Today, a student in a rural village can access the same lectures as a student at a prestigious university, and a working professional can upskill at midnight. This democratization of information is not merely a convenience; it is a fundamental shift in how society operates. It empowers individuals to pursue careers, hobbies, and self-improvement that were previously out of reach. Furthermore, the argument that computers harm hand-eye coordination is outdated. While static video games are often blamed, modern interactive software and virtual reality are actually being used in therapy to improve motor skills and cognitive flexibility. The digital realm is a gymnasium for the mind, offering puzzles, simulations, and complex problem-solving scenarios that keep our neural pathways active and adaptable. Secondly, computers have revolutionized human connection, particularly for those who are isolated. For individuals with chronic illnesses, social anxiety, or those living in remote areas, online communities are not a substitute for face-to-face interaction; they are a lifeline. They provide a space where people can find belonging, share experiences, and receive support that might not be available in their immediate physical environment. While critics worry about "online friends" replacing real ones, we must recognize that friendship is not strictly defined by physical proximity. The ability to video call a relative across the ocean, to collaborate with colleagues in different time zones, or to join a global conversation about a shared passion creates a fabric of global empathy. We are becoming more aware of issues on the other side of the world, fostering a sense of shared humanity that was previously difficult to achieve. However, I do not dismiss the valid concerns regarding sedentary lifestyles and the displacement of nature. It is true that excessive screen time can lead to physical inactivity and mental fatigue. But this is a problem of moderation and design, not an inherent flaw of the technology itself. The solution is not to ban computers, but to educate ourselves and our children on digital hygiene.

title: Does compatibilism imply that an AI agent has free will?
text: I have been grappling with the implications of compatibilist definitions of free will in the context of artificial intelligence, and I find myself at an impasse. The standard compatibilist position, as articulated by philosophers like Daniel Dennett and Harry Frankfurt, holds that free will is not incompatible with determinism, provided that an agent’s actions are the result of their own internal processes—such as desires, beliefs, and intentions—without external coercion or compulsion. In this view, an agent has free will if they could have done otherwise only in the sense that they would have done otherwise had their desires been different. The key criterion is not metaphysical indeterminacy, but rather the alignment of action with the agent’s own evaluative hierarchy. This raises a pressing question for contemporary AI, particularly large language models and autonomous decision-making systems. If we adopt a strict compatibilist framework, do these systems possess free will? On one hand, one might argue that since AI agents are deterministic systems (at least at the computational level, barring stochastic sampling in output generation), they lack the "ultimate responsibility" that some libertarians demand. However, compatibilism explicitly rejects the need for ultimate, non-causal responsibility. Instead, it asks: does the AI agent act according to its own "internal" governance? Consider an advanced AI agent designed to manage a smart city’s traffic flow. It receives sensor data, processes it through a complex neural network, and issues commands to traffic lights. Its actions are determined by its programming, training data, and current state. Are these "internal" to the agent? If we define the system boundary to include its weights, architecture, and real-time state, then its decisions are, in a functional sense, generated by the system itself. It is not being pushed by an external hand at every step; rather, it is responding to inputs based on its own learned heuristics. In this light, the AI appears to meet the compatibilist criteria of "sourcehood"—the action originates from the agent’s internal causal structure. However, critics might counter that the AI lacks "authenticity" or "moral agency" because its "desires" are hardcoded or learned from human data, not autonomously generated through a reflective process. Frankfurt’s hierarchy of desires distinguishes between first-order desires (I want ice cream) and second-order volitions (I want to want ice cream). Human free will, in this model, requires a reflective capacity to endorse or reject our first-order impulses. Most current AI systems lack this reflective, second-order evaluation in any meaningful sense. They do not "want" to want their outputs; they simply predict them. Does the absence of second-order volition disqualify an AI from compatibilist free will, or is this a feature specific to biological cognition that is not a necessary condition for the concept of free will itself? Furthermore, the issue of "could have done otherwise" becomes tricky. If an AI’s next token is determined by probability distributions over its learned patterns, is it "able" to choose a different token?

title: Condemnation
text: In the rich‑but‑rotting city of Aethelburg, where tall towers of the rich stab through a sky forever choked with smog, Archivist Elara Vance finds a truth that turns her world upside down. For as long as anyone can remember, the city’s wealth has been paid for by the “Condemned” – people whose bodies have been altered so they feel all the pain and misery of everyone else. Their suffering is drained and neutralized, letting the folks above live in comfort. While digitizing the old records of the city’s founding, Elara comes across the original charter: the Condemnation wasn’t a punishment for criminals at all, it was a lottery, a kind of human sacrifice dressed up as justice. The first Condemned was actually a hero who volunteered to save the city from a plague, and the system has been twisted ever since. The Ministry of Purity, the ruthless agency that keeps the city’s fragile peace, puts a target on her back as soon as she learns the truth. Forced to run from her safe, cloistered life, Elara dives into the Undercity – a tangled maze of tunnels beneath Aethelburg where outcasts and the descendants of those who slipped past the lottery have made a home. There she meets Kaelen, a bitter, scar‑covered ex‑enforcer for the Ministry who fled after being ordered to condemn a child. He’s haunted by what he did, and he sees a flicker of redemption in Elara’s hopeful naiveté, even though he thinks her mission is doomed. Together they hatch a plan to break into the Sanctum, the Ministry’s supposedly impenetrable headquarters, and broadcast the original charter for all to hear. Their trek takes them through the city’s underbelly – forgotten maintenance shafts, bustling illegal markets where gossip is the most valuable thing, and other hidden corners. All the while Commander Lyra, a brilliant and fanatical officer of the Ministry, hunts them. Lyra believes the Condemnation is a necessary evil, a utilitarian fix that keeps chaos at bay. To her, Elara isn’t a hero; she’s a terrorist who could throw the whole city into anarchy. As they spend time together, Elara sees just how guilty Kaelen feels and how the physical and emotional scars he carries shape him. She also gets a harrowing look at the Condemned when she visits the “Reservoir,” a secret facility where they’re kept in a constant, numbed state of agony. Seeing that, she hardens into something else entirely – no longer a quiet scholar but a determined rebel. The climax erupts in the Sanctum’s central broadcast tower. Elara and Kaelen manage to get past the security, but Lyra is waiting. In a tense showdown, Lyra argues that exposing the truth will make the city collapse because its citizens aren’t ready to face the horror behind their comfort. Elara retorts that a society built on a lie is already broken. Kaelen sacrifices himself, holding off Lyra’s forces long enough for Elara to upload the charter to the city‑wide network.

title: Crazy
text: My neighbor's dog is going crazy. It's barking at a leaf that fell hours ago and won't stop. My mom's ironing the same shirt again, and it's already perfectly creased. That's just how it is in this house - nothing happens just once, everything keeps repeating. I knew a guy who spent thirty years building a boat in his basement. It was too big to fit out the door. He said the sea would find him eventually. And he was right, the water table under our town was rising. There's a woman on the corner who counts cars that turn left. She keeps track in a notebook. She has a system, and she's got her reasons. I once asked her what the numbers meant, and she looked at me like I was an idiot. The thing is, you can't just call it what it is. You've got to keep it vague. The guy who talks to pigeons in the square is just having a conversation. The woman who saves every newspaper is just trying to remember things that the rest of us have forgotten. I've got a drawer full of keys that don't fit anything. And I always check the stove a bunch of times before bed. The dog's still barking, and the iron's still hot. The boat's still stuck in the basement. We're all a little off, I guess. We're all tuned into different frequencies. The trick is to just go along with it, to find a way to make it work. You've got to turn the dial down low and hum along with the noise. So let the dog keep barking. Let the woman count her cars. Let the guy in the basement work on his boat. Let the pigeons talk back. The world's full of people who are a little lost, who've got their own ways of navigating. And still, the sun comes up every morning. I check the stove a few times, then I go to sleep. And I dream about boats and basements filling up with water, and numbers that finally add up to something. The dog's stopped barking now. The leaf's just lying there. The woman's gone home to write down her numbers. Somewhere, someone's painting a boat the color of a sea they've never seen. And somewhere, someone's notebook is filling up with light. We're not messed up, we're just...different. We're tuned into different frequencies. We're the noise and the music. We're the crease that won't flatten, the key that doesn't fit, the boat that's just waiting for the water to come.

title: Dollar slides ahead of New Year
text: The US dollar slipped a bit against most of the big currencies on Monday. Traders were winding down the year and cutting back on safe‑haven bets, and the thin holiday trading made any moves look bigger. The dollar index – that number that compares the greenback to six peers – dropped about 0.4%. At the same time the euro nudged up 0.5%, the pound rose roughly 0.3%, and the yen strengthened enough to push the dollar down 0.6% against it. People in the market said this wasn’t about a single piece of news so much as a little portfolio reshuffle before the year ends. With many desks down to just a few people and a handful of major markets either shut or closing early, even small flows had a big impact. “Liquidity is very poor, so it doesn’t take much to move the dollar,” said a currency strategist at a European bank. “Everyone is taking profits on long‑dollar positions and squaring up before the holidays.” The dollar had been getting a lift all year because most folks thought the Fed would keep rates higher longer than other central banks. But recent data has made it look like inflation is cooling, and policymakers might be able to ease up in the months ahead. Traders are now betting more on rate cuts, which hurts the dollar’s yield edge. Lower US bond yields – the 10‑year Treasury slipped a bit – also weighed on the currency. In Europe, the euro got a little push from a modest rise in risk appetite and from the idea that the ECB may be slower to cut rates than some investors expected. The pound got a boost from end‑of‑year demand for sterling, although analysts warned the UK economy is still fragile. The yen, which has been all over the place this year, benefited from the dip in US yields and from safe‑haven buying tied to geopolitical worries. Emerging‑market currencies gave a mixed picture. Some high‑yielding currencies saw buyers looking for returns, while others stayed under pressure because of worries about global growth and debt. The dollar’s fall gave only a tiny bit of relief to countries that owe a lot in dollars, since financing costs are still high. Commodity‑linked currencies like the Australian and Canadian dollars inched up, helped by firmer oil and metal prices. The Swiss franc, another classic safe haven, was basically flat. Traders noted that month‑end and quarter‑end portfolio tweaks also played a part, and that trading volumes would stay low throughout the holiday stretch. Analysts cautioned not to read too much into the dollar’s end‑of‑year softness. With trading light until the first full week of January, the next big focus will be fresh US employment and inflation data and whatever the central banks say. “The next big move will depend on whether the data confirms the easing narrative,” said another strategist.

title: I2C SDA line acts erratically, requiring touch to work
text: I’m messing around with a tiny sensor board that uses an STM32F103 (the “blue‑pill” clone) as the I2C master. It talks to a BME280 breakout at 100 kHz over a couple of jumper wires that are only about 10 cm long. Both SDA and SCL have 4.7 kΩ pull‑ups to 3.3 V. Everything shares the same 3.3 V LDO and the grounds are tied together. The symptom Most of the time the bus just dies. When I call HAL_I2C_IsDeviceReady() I get HAL_ERROR. Probing the lines with an oscilloscope shows SCL sitting high while SDA is stuck low. It’s as if something is holding SDA down forever, either a device that got stuck in the middle of a transfer or the master that never lets go. Weirdly, the whole thing comes back to life the moment I touch the SDA line with my finger (or press a finger across SDA and the nearby ground pad on the breakout). After a touch the bus works fine for a while—sometimes minutes—then it quits again and another touch fixes it. It’s completely repeatable. What I’ve already tried Swapped the BME280 for another identical board – same problem. Played with the pull‑up values: 10 kΩ → 4.7 kΩ → 2.2 kΩ – no real improvement. Cut the wire length down to roughly 5 cm and even twisted SDA with GND – a tiny bit better, but it still crashes. Measured with a multimeter: before HAL_I2C_Init() both lines sit at 3.3 V; after the first failed transfer SDA hovers around 0.4 V. Added a 100 nF decoupling capacitor right on the breakout’s VCC – no effect. Slowed the bus to 50 kHz and even 10 kHz – the failure looks identical. Double‑checked that the STM32 pins are set to open‑drain AF, not push‑pull. Ran the usual “clock out 9 pulses on SCL” recovery before each transaction (using HAL_I2C_DeInit() / HAL_I2C_Init()). It helps occasionally, but not consistently, and it still doesn’t explain the finger‑touch magic. Made sure the BME280’s SDO pin is hard‑wired to GND, giving it address 0x76. Looked at the pull‑up voltage on the breakout with a scope: it’s clean, but when SDA is stuck there’s a noticeable ~1.5 V plateau on the rising edge of SCL, as if something is fighting the pull‑up. Why the finger thing bugs me Touching SDA only adds a few tens of picofarads of body capacitance to ground, which should actually make the edges slower, not better. So I don’t think this is a rise‑time issue. It feels more like the touch is draining some stray charge or providing a weak path that lets the line get out of a latched state. Touching the metal shield of the USB connector usually does nothing, so the effect seems specific to the SDA net rather than a generic grounding or ESD quirk. What could be going on? Is the BME280 latching up internally? Could there be a missing ground reference between the two boards?

text: Dear Editor, I think it's fair to say that computers have changed our lives more than any other invention. They're everywhere - in homes, schools, and workplaces - and we rely on them for just about everything. Some people worry that they're making us lonely, lazy, and antisocial, but I think that's only half the story. Used sensibly, computers can actually enrich our lives, help us learn new things, and connect us with others in amazing ways. Take education, for example. Computer games and software can help kids develop skills like problem-solving, creativity, and hand-eye coordination. When kids design animations or code simple programs, they're learning valuable skills that will serve them well beyond the screen. And it's not just kids - adults can learn new things too. Online courses make it possible for people to study at any time, and language apps can help us communicate with others in their own language. Computers are basically teaching machines, and they're really good at it. Some people also think that computers stifle curiosity, but I don't think that's true. With just a few clicks, you can explore museums, watch live footage from around the world, or read about your local history. It's amazing how much information is out there, and it's all just a click away. This isn't just about wasting time - it's about learning and discovery. Computers also help us connect with others. Some people say they make us isolated, but I think that's just not true. Grandparents can video-call their grandkids who live far away, friends can share photos and stories, and people with rare illnesses can find support groups online. For people who are housebound or shy, the internet can be a lifeline. These are real relationships, and they're worth nurturing. Of course, there are risks to too much screen time. We need to make sure we're not spending too much time sitting around and not enough time getting exercise and fresh air. But that's not the computer's fault - it's up to us to use them sensibly. We can set limits, balance screen time with outdoor activities, and use technology with our families rather than alone. Lots of families already do this, and it brings them closer together. Computers have also made a big difference in practical ways. Doctors can consult with specialists around the world, farmers can monitor their crops with sensors, and small businesses can reach customers far beyond their local area. These benefits affect all of us, whether or not we use computers ourselves. In short, computers are just tools - they're not good or bad in themselves. It's up to us to use them wisely. I think we should see them as a way to learn, connect, and explore the world, rather than something to be feared. If we use them sensibly and balance them with other parts of our lives, I think they'll prove to be one of the greatest benefits our society has ever known. Yours faithfully, A Concerned Reader

title: Copyright ownership and implied license for an unpaid volunteer’s independent report
text: I spent about eight months volunteering with a small environmental nonprofit. I never got paid or signed any contract. I started helping out with general tasks after they put out a call for volunteers. Then, the director emailed me and asked if I'd be willing to research and write a report on a regulatory issue that affected their mission. The email was pretty informal - something like "we'd love it if you could put together a report on X for us, no one here has time, and you know the topic best." We didn't discuss payment, copyright, or who owned the work. I did the work on my own time, using my own computer, and they only gave me a few public documents and some internal notes. I ended up producing a 40-page report with my own analysis, citations, and recommendations. I sent a draft to the director, and we discussed it a couple of times. They gave me feedback and asked me to make changes, which I did. Eventually, I sent them what I thought was the final version. I didn't include a copyright notice or register it with anyone. The organization later put a PDF of the report on their website, with my name as author, and used excerpts in grant applications and comments to a government agency. At the time, I was fine with that - I was just trying to help out. We didn't have any written agreement about who owned the work, and no one ever told me that they owned it or that I couldn't use it elsewhere. Lately, we've had a disagreement over some governance issues, and I've left the organization. Now, I want to publish the report myself, maybe through a small press, and possibly adapt parts of it into articles. But the organization says that the report is "their property" because I wrote it for them as a volunteer, and that I need their permission to republish it. They also claim that they have an exclusive license to the work because they directed it and used it. I don't agree with that. I'm trying to figure out my legal position before I respond or take further steps. Specifically, I want to know: 1. Who owns the copyright to the report under U.S. law? As an unpaid volunteer, not an employee, and with no written agreement, does the work-for-hire doctrine apply to me? Does it matter that the director suggested the topic and gave feedback? 2. If I own the copyright, did I give the organization permission to use the report by implication? What do courts look at in cases like this? Can they revoke that permission, and what happens to copies they've already distributed? 3. If there is an implied license, can it be exclusive? I never agreed to exclusivity, and I never promised not to use my own work elsewhere. Is the organization's claim of an "exclusive license by implication" valid? 4.

title: Army of Darkness
text: Sam Raimi’s *Army of Darkness* is a wild, blood‑soaked, totally over‑the‑top movie that caps off the *Evil Dead* trilogy. *Evil Dead II* nailed the mix of slapstick and straight‑up horror, but the third ride throws that out the window and goes full‑on medieval fantasy, seen through a kind of Looney Tunes‑style filter. It’s a film that revels in being ridiculous, swapping the cramped cabin terror for sprawling, chaotic battlefields in a messed‑up past. At the center of the madness is Bruce Campbell, who probably gives the best performance of his career as Ash Williams. By now Ash has gone from scared cabin‑dweller to a reluctant, chin‑pushed action hero. He’s the every‑guy thrown into a world of magic and skeletons, wielding a chainsaw for a hand and a double‑barrel shotgun. Campbell’s charm is what keeps everything moving; he can flip from dead‑pan sarcasm to full‑blown bravado in a beat, so the movie stays manic but never loses its core character. He’s not just a hero—he’s a hero who’s constantly confused, annoyed, and way out of his league, which makes his wins oddly satisfying. Visually the film is a burst of energy. Raimi’s famous shaky‑camera work and crazy POV shots are everywhere, turning even the simplest action into a frantic experience. The set design, despite a shoestring budget, feels surprisingly lived‑in and detailed, even if it’s filled with deadites that look intentionally grotesque. The practical effects steal the show—stop‑motion, puppets, heavy prosthetic makeup—all give the gore a weight and a physicality that CGI just can’t match. Those ridiculous fights somehow feel grounded by that tactile feel. The shift from horror to adventure is handled with a wink. Sure, die‑hard fans might miss the tight tension of the earlier movies, but *Army of Darkness* works because it fully embraces its cult‑comedy vibe. It pokes fun at heroic fantasy while also loving it. The dialogue snaps, the pacing never quits, and the score adds a grand, over‑the‑top feel that perfectly parodies the epics of its day. In the end, *Army of Darkness* is pure, unfiltered fun. It’s a love letter to B‑movie style and a reminder that making movies can just be a blast. It doesn’t ask for you to think deeply; it just wants you to watch, laugh, and enjoy the absurdity. If you dig practical effects, slap‑stick action, or the sheer spectacle of a guy battling an undead army with a power tool, this movie is a must‑see. Loud, messy, and brilliantly imaginative, it’s a triumph of pure imagination.

title: Potato Gnocchi in Lemon-Butter Sauce with Scallops and Sea Urchin
text: This dish is all about showing off the best of the coast, with a mix of textures and flavors that complement each other. You've got your pillowy gnocchi made from scratch, your rich and briny sea urchin, and your tender scallops with a nice sear on them. The lemon butter sauce brings everything together, adding a bit of zing to cut through all the richness. Makes: 2 servings Prep time: About an hour, plus some time for the potatoes to dry out Cook time: 20 minutes Ingredients For the Potato Gnocchi: 1 lb big Russet potatoes (you want the starchy kind) 1 ½ cups special flour (Type 00) plus some extra for dusting 1 egg, beaten lightly ½ tsp fine sea salt A pinch of nutmeg, grated fresh For the Seafood: 6 large scallops, dried really well 3–4 oz fresh sea urchin (get the good stuff) 2 tbsp oil with a high smoke point (I use grapeseed or avocado) 1 tbsp unsalted butter (for searing) For the Lemon-Butter Sauce: 4 tbsp unsalted European-style butter, cubed and chilled Juice and zest of ½ lemon (organic, if you can get it) ¼ cup dry white wine (something like Pinot Grigio or Sauvignon Blanc) 1 small shallot, minced fine 2 tbsp pasta water (reserved from boiling gnocchi) Some micro-greens or chives for garnish Flaky sea salt (Maldon is nice) Instructions 1. Make the Gnocchi: Boil some whole potatoes in salty water until they're tender. Drain and peel them while they're still warm. Then mash them up with a potato ricer onto a clean surface. Spread the mashed potatoes out so they can cool down and lose some moisture. Once they've cooled a bit, sprinkle some flour and salt on them. Make a well in the center and add your beaten egg and nutmeg. Fold everything together gently, then knead just until it forms a dough. Roll it out into long ropes, cut into 1-inch pieces, and press them with a fork if you like. Set them aside on a floured tray. 2. Sear the Scallops: Season your dried scallops with salt just before cooking. Heat some oil in a stainless steel or cast-iron pan over high heat until it's shimmering. Add the scallops, making sure they don't touch. Cook for 2 minutes on one side, until they get a nice golden-brown crust. Flip them, add some butter to the pan, and baste them for 30 seconds. Then take them out and put them on a warm plate. 3. The Lemon-Butter Sauce: In a wide pan, sauté some minced shallot in a bit of butter over medium heat until it's translucent. Add some white wine and scrape up any browned bits. Reduce the liquid by half, then turn the heat down low and whisk in your chilled butter, one cube at a time. Stir in some lemon juice and zest. 4. Assembly: Boil your gnocchi in salty water until they float to the surface.

title: Man on the Moon
text: Milosh Forman’s *Man on the Moon* lives in that messy, beautiful spot between a straight‑up biography and a deep‑dive character study. Most biopics just march from birth to death like an assembly line, but Forman goes for something ragged and rhythmic, trying to match the very chaos of his subject: Andy Kaufman. The movie never tells us exactly who Kaufman was, and that refusal actually feels truer than any neat documentary could ever be. Jim Carrey gives what might be his most disciplined, most transformative turn yet. Usually we see Carrey’s talent in his wild, rubber‑face antics—a sort of superhero ability to stretch his features for jokes. Here he pulls that energy back, using it for a creepy, inward performance instead. He nails Kaufman’s deep loneliness and his obsessive need to blur the line between act and real life. Carrey isn’t just “playing” Andy; he’s slipping into the manic frequency Andy lived on. In the quieter scenes with Lynne Loxton (Lauren Holly), you can see vulnerability in his eyes that keeps the whole thing from spinning into pure oddness. The film’s structure is deliberately jumpy, hopping around different periods of Kaufman’s career and his relationship with Loxton. That non‑linear style isn’t random—it’s meant to imitate watching Kaufman himself. When you saw a Kaufman routine you never knew if you were watching a joke, a prank, or a genuine breakdown. By chopping the story up, Forman forces us into that same confusion. We never quite know when the “character” stops and the “man” starts, which feels like the most honest way to show a guy whose whole life was about subverting identity. The supporting cast is just as strong, with actors playing exaggerated, almost cartoonish versions of real people, adding to the film’s surreal vibe. It captures the gritty, gritty energy of the late ’70s‑early ’80s comedy scene without turning into a pure nostalgia trip. Instead, that backdrop becomes a lens for looking at the artist’s isolation. Kaufman comes across as someone who saw the world as a stage, only to find himself in a vacuum once the curtain fell. If there’s a flaw, it’s that the movie sometimes loses its tonal footing. One minute you’re in the high‑concept absurdity of his sketches, the next you’re hit with tender, heartbreaking moments from his personal life, and the shift can feel abrupt. Then again, maybe that jolt is intentional. Life, like Kaufman’s art, isn’t a smooth glide from laughter to sorrow. In the end, *Man on the Moon* isn’t just a film about a comedian; it’s a meditation on the masks we wear and the heavy price of nonstop performance. It’s a messy, flawed, but deeply empathetic portrait that gets the point: the most interesting thing about a person isn’t their public act, but the mystery that lingers when the lights finally go down.

title: EU China arms ban 'to be lifted'
text: The European Union is finally going to lift its ban on selling arms and military tech to China. This is a big deal, and it marks a major change in how the EU relates to Beijing. The decision was made behind closed doors at a meeting of the European Council in Brussels. It's the result of months of intense debate and negotiation among member states. For almost 30 years, the EU has had strict rules against exporting military gear to China. This was mainly because of concerns about human rights in Hong Kong and Xinjiang, and China's growing military presence in the South China Sea. But now, some top officials say the world has changed a lot, and it's time for the EU to adjust. They're not trying to get on China's side, but rather to be more practical and strengthen economic ties in a time of global uncertainty. One senior diplomat said that the world isn't just divided into two camps anymore. To succeed in the 21st century, the EU needs to balance its values with the need to communicate and trade with China, which is the world's second-biggest economy. The ban will be lifted in stages, starting with things like advanced semiconductors and satellite navigation systems that can be used for both civilian and military purposes. The EU plans to keep a close eye on things to make sure they don't end up in China's military or surveillance programs. People across Europe have very different opinions about this decision. Leaders from France and Germany are mostly in favor, saying that cutting ties with China would hurt Europe's economy. They think that by trading with China, the EU can have some influence over Chinese industries. On the other hand, officials from some Eastern European countries and the Baltic states are worried. They think that easing restrictions on China could make Beijing bolder and weaken the security of the Indo-Pacific region, which they see as connected to Europe's stability. A spokesperson for a security think tank in Brussels said that this is a huge risk. By lifting the ban, the EU is betting that its regulations are strong enough to prevent China from misusing the technology. It's a high-stakes gamble with the future of global security. China is happy about the decision, saying it's a step towards normalizing relations and rejecting what it calls outdated Cold War thinking. Now that the EU is about to make the announcement official, everyone is watching the US. The White House hasn't said much yet, but analysts think this could cause tension between the EU and the US, since America is still trying to limit China's military growth.

title: Seperating compute and storage with per-tenant databases
text: I’m building a multi‑tenant SaaS platform that has to crunch a lot of analytics data. The biggest rule we have to follow is keeping each customer’s data completely separate – the compliance folks demand it – but we also need to be able to grow the compute side without having to grow storage at the same time. Right now we’re leaning toward a “one database per tenant” approach. The idea is to split things up: the storage side will be a bunch of managed PostgreSQL instances (or separate schemas inside a big cluster), and the compute side will be a set of stateless microservices running on Kubernetes. The trouble starts when we think about the operational cost of running hundreds, maybe thousands, of individual databases while still trying to be resource‑efficient. If we give every tenant its own database to get the best isolation, we end up with a lot of “empty space.” Most tenants are tiny and sit idle, so we’d be paying for huge chunks of IOPS and RAM that barely get used. On the other hand, the big “whale” customers need massive vertical scaling, which could push us to put them on dedicated hardware and break the uniformity of our deployment scripts. So I’m toying with a hybrid model: bundle the small tenants together in shared clusters (using schema‑level isolation) and give the high‑value or high‑load tenants their own dedicated instances. That adds a layer of complexity to the data‑access side though. Our app would have to know which tenant_id maps to which connection string or endpoint, and we’d need a smooth way to move a tenant from a shared cluster to its own instance without any downtime. Specifically, I’m looking for advice on a few things: 1. Abstraction Layers: In a setup where compute and storage are separate, what’s the best way to handle connection pooling? With 1,000 tenants, if each pool keeps a few idle connections we could hit the database’s connection limits fast. Should we go with a sidecar per tenant (something like PgBouncer), or use a single centralized proxy? 2. Schema Evolution: How do you roll out migrations across a scattered storage landscape? When a breaking schema change is needed, updating thousands of independent databases one by one feels risky – you could end up with half the world on the new version and half still on the old. Is it smarter to treat migrations as an async, eventually‑consistent process, or do they have to be tightly coupled with the compute deployment? 3. Scaling Granularity: When a particular tenant becomes a bottleneck, the ideal move is to boost just their storage performance without touching anyone else. In a cloud‑native world, is it better to crank up the underlying disk throughput (EBS, PVCs) or to spin the whole database up to a bigger instance type? And how do we automate that “rebalancing” without manual steps? 4.

title: Julia Child'S Duck A L'Orange
text: Julia Child's Duck à l'Orange is a classic French dish that's hard to beat - a beautifully roasted duck with a shiny, tangy orange sauce is just wonderful. Don't worry if it seems intimidating, just take your time and remember that you can always adjust the sauce. Bon appétit! Ingredients 1 duck, about 4½ to 5 pounds, with neck and giblets Salt and black pepper 3 large oranges 1 carrot, sliced 1 onion, sliced 1 tablespoon sugar 3 tablespoons red wine vinegar 2 cups chicken or duck stock 1½ tablespoons cornstarch or arrowroot 2 tablespoons unsalted butter 2 tablespoons orange liqueur (optional) Serves 4 to 6 Instructions Roasting the duck: Preheat your oven to 375°F. Get rid of the giblets and save the liver for later. Cut off the wing tips and extra fat from the duck's cavity. Tie the duck up so it roasts evenly. Now, prick the skin all over with a fork, especially around the thighs and breast - just the fat layer, not the meat. Season the cavity and skin with salt and pepper. Put the duck in a roasting pan, breast-up, on a rack. Roast for about 1½ hours, pouring off the fat every 20 minutes or so. Save this fat - it's great for frying potatoes! The duck is done when the skin is brown and the legs move easily. Remove the duck to a platter and keep it warm. The orange preparation: While the duck roasts, peel strips of zest from two oranges and cut them into fine strips. Blanch them in boiling water for 5 minutes, then drain and set aside. Squeeze the juice from two oranges - you'll need about ½ cup. Peel the third orange and cut it into segments. The sauce: Pour out the fat from the roasting pan, add the sliced carrot and onion, and brown them lightly. Deglaze with a bit of stock, scraping up the browned juices - that's where the flavor is! Strain the liquid into a saucepan and add the rest of the stock, simmering to reduce a bit. Make your caramel: boil the sugar and vinegar until it's a deep brown and smells like caramel. Pour in the orange juice - be careful, it will sputter! Then stir the mixture into your sauce. Blend the cornstarch with a bit of cold water and whisk it into the sauce. Simmer until it thickens, then off the heat, swirl in the butter and liqueur (if using). Add the blanched zest and taste, adjust the seasoning as needed. It should be a balance of sweet, bitter, and tart. To serve: Carve the duck, remove the legs and slice the breast meat. Arrange the meat on a platter, scatter the orange segments around it, and spoon some sauce over the duck. Serve the rest of the sauce on the side, with rice or potatoes and a salad.

title: Just another lovely call to the IRS 😆
text: So I got one of those cheerful CP14 letters last week telling me I still owed $1,847 for my 2022 return. Fun fact: I have a bank statement that shows the payment cleared back in April 2023. But hey, IRS, right? I thought it would be a snap. “You already have my money, here’s the confirmation number—have a nice day.” Yeah, right. LMAO. I called at 7:02 a.m. because apparently you have to hit the line the second it opens or you’re doomed. The estimated wait time? Forty‑five minutes to an hour. No problem. I tossed on my headphones, brewed coffee, and prepared for some quality time with the world’s most soul‑sucking hold music—a fifteen‑second loop of soft jazz that drags on forever, punctuated every few minutes by a robotic lady saying “your call is important to us.” If it were, someone would’ve answered already. An hour and twelve minutes later, a real person finally appeared: Marcus from accounts. I told him the whole story, he pulled up my file, and said, “Yep, I see the payment, no problem!” I was almost crying with joy. Then he added, “You’ll need to talk to collections. Let me transfer you, one moment.” Marcus, you’re a good guy and I know it’s not your fault, but the hold music roared back for another thirty‑five minutes while I cursed the heavens. The next rep picked up and, surprise, she had no record of my payment—nothing at all, the exact opposite of what Marcus said. She asked me to read the confirmation number off my statement, which I did. She put me on hold “just a quick moment” to check something. That “quick moment” stretched to twenty‑two minutes, then the line switched to the “please call back later, we’re experiencing unusually high call volume” message and hung up on me. Two hours and nine minutes gone, and all I got was an intimate familiarity with that jazz loop. I called right back, feeling possessed. The estimated wait time now read “greater than 2 hours.” Greater than what? They didn’t even bother giving me a number. So I did the only sensible thing: I called from my cell and from the house phone at the same time, hoping to halve the hold time. The landline won after a little over an hour. The rep finally said the payment WAS received, but it had been posted to the wrong tax year. The only fix? Mail in a written request with copies of everything. Mail! In 2025! And they said it could take eight to twelve weeks to process—maybe. Meanwhile, penalties and interest keep stacking up on money they already have, money they apparently lost, and now I have to snail‑mail a polite pleading letter asking them to find it. I really don’t get how an agency that collects trillions can operate like a Blockbuster that misplaced its entire rental log. And before anyone says “just use the online tools”—I did.

title: South Park: Bigger, Longer & Uncut
text: I first saw this movie in a theater the summer it came out, and I've been raving about it ever since. People might find it crude, obscene, and full of curse words, but to me, it's a clever musical that takes a sharp swipe at censorship and moral panic. The premise is ridiculously simple, which is what makes it brilliant. Some kids sneak into an R-rated movie, pick up some new words, and their parents freak out, declaring war on Canada. It sounds absurd, and it is, but that's the point. The creators, Parker and Stone, get that moral panic is just that - absurd. Every adult in the movie overreacts by blaming someone else, and that's what the plot is built on. The parents blame Canada, the government blames the movie makers, and everyone scrambles to avoid taking responsibility. The song "Blame Canada" is hilarious on the surface, but the lyrics are actually pretty insightful - "we must blame them and cause a fuss before somebody thinks of blaming us." It's like they're holding up a mirror to American politics. The songs in this movie are surprisingly good. I mean, "Uncle F*a" is filthy, but in a parody kind of way. And "It's Easy, Mmmkay" is a legitimately well-done number with some great rhymes. And then there's "Up There," Satan's big ballad, which is played completely straight and works because Parker and Stone actually know what they're doing. I was thrilled when "Blame Canada" got an Oscar nomination - it's like the Academy was honoring a song that's all about scapegoating, without even realizing it. There's this subplot with Satan and Saddam Hussein that's still hilarious to me. Satan as a sensitive soul trapped in a crappy relationship with Saddam is weirdly touching, and it feeds into this ending that gives Kenny, the kid who always dies, some actual emotional payoff. I didn't expect to feel anything from a South Park movie, but there I was, a little moved. It's ridiculous, but it's true. What impresses me on rewatch is how tight the movie is. It's barely 80 minutes long, and every joke and musical number serves the story. The animation is deliberately cheap, but the writing is anything but. Gags come at you from all directions, and the movie stays one step ahead of you. The great irony is that a film arguing against censorship had to fight the ratings board to get released. But the argument holds up - the kids' real problem wasn't the swearing, it was the adults who were too busy pointing fingers to actually parent. That message still holds up today. This movie is crude on the surface, but razor-sharp underneath. I'd give it 10/10, and I'm a fan of "Uncle F*a" forever.

text: Dear Editor, I’m writing to join the conversation about computers and how they’re changing our everyday lives. A lot of your readers seem to think these machines are pulling us away from exercise, the outdoors, and each other. I get that worry, but I honestly think that when we use computers sensibly they do way more good than harm – and I’d like to convince your readers to see them for the amazing tools they really are. First, think about what a computer puts in reach of every family in our town. A kid can explore the Great Barrier Reef or the ruins of ancient Rome without ever buying a plane ticket. A student stuck on algebra can find clear, patient explanations any time of day. When my classmates and I dug into a local‑history project, we pulled up photos and newspaper clippings that would have sat untouched in a dusty basement. My own grandmother, who lives three hundred miles away, now watches my little brother’s birthday parties on video calls and no longer feels cut off from us. Distance used to separate families; now it only separates bodies, not hearts. Add the practical skills—typing, research, hand‑eye coordination from games—that employers now expect, and it’s obvious the computer isn’t a luxury; it’s a doorway. Some people say screen time is time stolen from fresh air and friendship. But the problem is our choices, not the machine. A hammer can build a bookshelf or smash a window; we don’t blame the hammer. If someone spends a whole weekend inside, the fix isn’t to ban computers, it’s to build better habits around them. In fact, the same computer that can tempt us to stay indoors also gets us out the door: my family has used ours to discover hiking trails we never knew existed, to check the weather before a picnic, and to learn which birds visit our feeder each spring. The tech didn’t replace our walk in the park—it made it better. The same goes for family life. Critics claim computers mute the dinner table, and yes, that can happen in homes without rules. In my house, though, the computer has sparked more conversation than it has killed: we share funny videos, plan vacations together, and my parents use it to help me with homework they don’t remember how to do themselves. Screens only become antisocial when we let them. A family that agrees on sensible limits—say, an hour after homework, none at the dinner table—quickly finds the computer, like the TV before it, can be a companion to family life rather than a rival. I’m not saying anyone should live online 24/7. Exercise, sunlight, face‑to‑face friendship are as essential as food, and no reasonable person would give those up. My point is simple: stop treating the computer as the enemy and see it for what it is—a tool whose worth depends entirely on the hand that wields it.

title: Swedish Meatballs With Gravy And Lingonberry Preserves
text: Swedish Meatballs With Gravy and Lingonberry Preserves *Serves 4–6* Ingredients For the meatballs 1 pound ground beef Half a pound ground pork Half a cup whole milk Half a cup fine breadcrumbs 1 small onion, finely grated 1 large egg Half a teaspoon ground all-spice Half a teaspoon ground white pepper A quarter teaspoon ground nutmeg Half a teaspoon kosher salt, plus extra for seasoning For the creamy brown gravy 3 Tablespoons unsalted butter 3 Tablespoons all-purpose flour 2 cups beef or veal stock, warmed Half a cup heavy cream 1 Tablespoon Worcestershire sauce 1 teaspoon soy sauce, for color Half a teaspoon Dijon mustard Salt and black pepper, to taste For the finishing touches 2 Tablespoons butter, for sautéing Chopped fresh parsley, optional 1 cup lingonberry preserves, served on the side Equipment Large mixing bowl Small skillet Medium saucepan Wooden spoon Baking sheet, optional Fine-mesh strainer, for the gravy Directions 1. Prepare the meatball mixture Mix breadcrumbs and milk in a bowl. Let it sit for 2 minutes. Add ground beef, pork, onion, egg, all-spice, pepper, nutmeg, and salt. Mix gently with your hands until just combined. 2. Shape the meatballs Use damp hands to roll the mixture into balls, about 1 inch in diameter. You should get around 30–35 meatballs. 3. Brown the meatballs Heat 2 Tablespoons of butter in a large skillet over medium-high. Add meatballs in batches if needed. Cook, turning occasionally, until browned on all sides, about 4–5 minutes. Transfer to a plate. 4. Make the roux Reduce heat to medium and add the remaining 3 Tablespoons butter. Sprinkle flour over butter and stir for 2–3 minutes, until golden brown. 5. Create the gravy Whisk in warm stock, a little at a time, until smooth. Whisk until the sauce thickens, about 4–5 minutes. Stir in heavy cream, Worcestershire sauce, soy sauce, and mustard. Simmer for 2 minutes. 6. Finish the meatballs in the sauce Return meatballs to the skillet and simmer, covered, for 10–12 minutes, or until cooked through. Taste and adjust seasoning as needed. 7. Serve Spoon gravy over meatballs on a platter. Add chopped parsley if you like. Serve with lingonberry preserves on the side. Tips & Variations Ground meat ratio: Try a 2:1 beef-to-pork ratio for a richer texture. Breadcrumbs: Use panko or make your own from stale bread. Gravy depth: Add a splash of brandy or tomato paste for complexity. Make-ahead: Freeze raw meatballs and thaw before cooking, or cook straight from frozen. This classic dish is perfect for a cozy dinner or a holiday spread.

text: Five-Spice Duck Tostada with Ginger-Chile Cream Dressing Serves 4 Ingredients For the Duck 2 pounds duck breast, skin on 1 ½ teaspoons Chinese five-spice powder 1 teaspoon sea salt ½ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper 1 tablespoon soy sauce 1 tablespoon hoisin sauce 1 teaspoon honey 1 tablespoon vegetable oil for searing For the Tostada Base 8 small corn tostada shells or make your own using 8-inch corn tortillas fried until crisp 1 cup shredded red cabbage ½ cup thinly sliced radishes ½ cup sliced cucumber ¼ cup torn fresh cilantro leaves 2 green onions, thinly sliced 1 avocado, sliced For the Ginger-Chile Cream Dressing ¾ cup sour cream or Greek yogurt 1 tablespoon grated fresh ginger 1 small red chile, seeds removed and finely minced 1 clove garlic, pressed 1 teaspoon lime zest 2 tablespoons freshly squeezed lime juice 1 teaspoon honey ¼ teaspoon toasted sesame oil Pinch of salt to taste 2 teaspoons chopped fresh mint, optional Garnish, optional Toasted sesame seeds Micro cilantro or micro basil Preparation 1. Marinate the Duck 1. Pat the duck breasts dry. Score the skin in a crosshatch pattern, being careful not to cut into the meat. 2. Mix five-spice powder, salt, pepper, soy sauce, hoisin sauce, and honey in a shallow dish. Rub the paste all over the duck, focusing on the skin side. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes or up to 4 hours. 2. Cook the Duck 1. Preheat the oven to 375°F. 2. Heat a heavy skillet over medium-high heat with some oil. 3. Place the duck breasts skin-side down and press gently. Cook for 6-8 minutes or until the skin is golden and releases easily. 4. Flip the breasts, sear for 2 minutes, then transfer to the oven. Whisk together sour cream, ginger, chile, garlic, lime zest, lime juice, honey, and sesame oil in a bowl. 2. Taste and add a pinch of salt. Thin with water or lime juice if needed. Top with sliced duck, radishes, cucumber, avocado, cilantro, and green onions. 4. Drizzle the ginger-chile cream dressing over the tostadas. 5. Sprinkle toasted sesame seeds and micro herbs, if desired. Serving & Tips Prepare the dressing while the duck rests. For extra crunch, bake tostada shells in a 400°F oven for 2 minutes. title: Warm Johnny Cakes With Blackberries
text: Warm Johnny Cakes With Blackberries Johnny cakes, or hoecakes, are a classic Southern comfort food that's really easy to make and super tasty. When you pair them with fresh blackberries, it's like a match made in heaven - the sweetness of the blackberries complements the slightly sweet cakes perfectly. This recipe makes about 4 servings, and it's great for breakfast or a snack. Ingredients For the Johnny Cakes 1 cup of cornmeal 1/2 cup of all-purpose flour 1 teaspoon of baking powder 1/2 teaspoon of salt 1/2 teaspoon of baking soda 1 large egg 1 cup of buttermilk 2 tablespoons of melted unsalted butter For the Blackberry Topping 2 cups of fresh blackberries 2 tablespoons of granulated sugar 1 tablespoon of lemon juice 1 tablespoon of cornstarch mixed with 1 tablespoon of water For Serving 2 tablespoons of melted butter Powdered sugar for dusting Maple syrup (optional) Instructions 1. Prepare the Johnny Cakes Batter In a big bowl, whisk together the cornmeal, flour, baking powder, salt, and baking soda. In a separate bowl, whisk together the egg, buttermilk, and melted butter. Pour the wet ingredients into the dry ingredients and stir until just combined - the batter should still be a bit lumpy. Let it rest for 10 minutes so the cornmeal can absorb some of the liquid. 2. Cook the Johnny Cakes Heat a large skillet or griddle over medium heat and add a bit of butter to grease it. For each johnny cake, pour about 1/4 cup of batter onto the skillet. Cook until bubbles form on the surface and the edges start to look set, about 3-4 minutes. Flip them over and cook for another 2-3 minutes, until they're golden brown and cooked through. Transfer the cooked johnny cakes to a plate and keep them warm while you cook the rest. 3. Make the Blackberry Topping In a medium saucepan, combine the blackberries, sugar, and lemon juice. Cook over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until the blackberries start to break down and release their juices, about 5 minutes. Stir in the cornstarch mixture and continue to cook until the mixture thickens, about 2-3 minutes. Remove from heat and set aside. 4. Warm the Johnny Cakes Brush the warm johnny cakes with melted butter and dust them lightly with powdered sugar. 5. Serve Place the johnny cakes on plates and spoon the blackberry topping over the top. If you like, you can drizzle a bit of maple syrup over the top too. Enjoy them while they're still warm! Tips You can make the blackberry topping ahead of time and reheat it gently before serving. If you want to get fancy, serve the johnny cakes with a dollop of whipped cream or a side of yogurt. If you don't have buttermilk, you can make a substitute by mixing 1 cup of milk with 1 tablespoon of lemon juice or vinegar, and letting it sit for 5 minutes.

title: How do Louisiana's Congressional runoffs conform to the common election date law?
text: In Louisiana, the way they run congressional elections – especially run‑offs – is different from most states, and that difference makes people wonder if it lines up with federal election rules, namely the Federal Uniform Date of General Elections Law (42 U.S.C. § 1973‑1). That law says every general election for a federal office has to happen on “the Tuesday next after the first Monday in November” of an even‑numbered year. But Louisiana’s take on run‑offs throws a curveball into that schedule. Louisiana uses a “jungle primary.” All the candidates, no matter what party they belong to, appear on the same ballot. If nobody gets more than half the votes, the top two face each other in a run‑off. That second round usually falls on the fourth Saturday after the primary – often after the federal election date the law requires. The big question is whether this set‑up, which can leave a federal seat undecided after the legally‑mandated election day, breaches the federal rule. A few points help sort this out: 1. Federal vs. State jurisdiction – The uniform‑date law is a federal rule, so states have to follow it when they hold federal elections. Still, states have long run their own election logistics, including how they handle run‑offs. 2. Historical precedent – Louisiana’s jungle primary has been around for decades and courts have upheld it. In *Tucker v. DB Bennett* (627 F.2d 397, 5th Cir. 1980), the Supreme Court backed the system, signaling that the courts see it as valid under state election law. 3. Practical implications – The run‑off makes sure the winner actually has a majority, which sounds democratic. On the flip side, it pushes the final outcome past the federal deadline and can create administrative headaches. 4. Potential conflicts – Even with the court backing, we still have to ask whether a post‑deadline run‑off can coexist with the federal requirement for a single, uniform election day. Some might argue it doesn’t. 5. Legal interpretations – Scholars who study election law often say the federal law’s goal is just to set a common date for the main general election, not to micromanage every state’s primary or run‑off. In other words, the uniform‑date rule may only apply to that first, required election day. All things considered, it’s worth digging into the legal framework and figuring out where the friction points are between Louisiana’s system and the federal statute. Run‑offs can be seen as a necessary follow‑up to guarantee a majority winner, but they also risk stepping outside the federal timeline. Since the MAX7219’s chip‑select is active‑low, I made sure the line is pulled high when idle with the internal pull‑up and also a 10 kΩ external pull‑up to VCC for extra stability. While this arrangement is typical in experimental sciences—where you often rely on the professor’s expensive laboratory equipment—recently introduced junior‑professorships have shifted expectations compared to a decade ago, when the habilitation was the sole path to a professorship under a tenured mentor. title: Does Western Philosophy Have Conceptual Overlaps with Buddhism?
text: I think I’ve noticed several conceptual overlaps between Buddhism and Western philosophy and science. What are good sources for comparing and contrasting Western ideas with Buddhism? Which Western works are thought to have been influenced by Eastern thought? Below I list a few speculated commonalities, based on my admittedly incomplete understanding. My knowledge of Buddhism comes mainly from the books of Thích Nhất Hạnh and Alan Watts, and from attending Pure‑Land services for a time. PSYCHOLOGY For example, mindfulness shares some affinities with cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT) and with metacognition. Mindfulness involves awareness of one’s thoughts; metacognition adds the ability to monitor and regulate those thoughts. In other words, thinking is not just a random firing of neurons to which we are oblivious. The Buddhist “second noble truth” links suffering to delusion, while CBT attributes emotional suffering to “cognitive distortions.” These distortions typically consist of a lack of present‑mindedness, fixation on the past or future, and a failure to consider events within their full context. LITERATURE When Hamlet asks Rosencrantz and Guildenstern why they would volunteer to go to a prison, they reply that they do not think of Denmark as a prison. Hamlet responds, “[T]here is nothing good or bad, but thinking makes it so.” Here “good” and “bad” refer to pleasure and pain and the degree to which they are experienced. CBT makes a similar claim: emotional suffering arises from the way we think about experiences rather than from the experiences themselves. Buddhism likewise attributes suffering to various delusions, and CBT labels the responsible mental habits “cognitive distortions.” In *The Picture of Dorian Gray*, Oscar Wilde writes, “To become a spectator of one’s own life is to escape the suffering of life.” One can be self‑aware in a third‑person sense, or in the first‑person sense of an “I.” Wilde seems to be linking a reduction of suffering to a diminishment of ego. Shortly before writing the novel he penned the foreword to a friend’s book on the *Tao Te Ching*, suggesting that his remark also touches on mindful self‑awareness—the capacity to remain present amid misfortune without being emotionally tormented. William Blake’s poem “The Human Form Divine” appears to echo the Buddhist notion of “blessed human existence.” His famous lines—“To see a world in a grain of sand / And a heaven in a wild flower / Hold infinity in the palm of your hand / And eternity in an hour”—evoke a sense of timelessness. Blake was evidently familiar with Vedic material, as discussed in *Awakenings: Blake and the Buddha*. PHILOSOPHY / EPISTEMOLOGY More significantly, Aristotle’s *Nicomachean Ethics* approaches morality by emphasizing character development rather than merely evaluating isolated actions. According to Aristotle, doing the right thing for the wrong reason makes one less ethical than the ideal. Western philosophy groups such approaches under virtue ethics. Both Aristotle and the Buddha can be placed within this tradition, since each stresses the cultivation of wholesome character as the foundation of ethical life.

title: Philosophy of concepts - can it be (gradually) expressed in type theory?
text: Reasoning in mathematics is straightforward and amenable to automation because every mathematical notion—whether it is an integer, a real number, a derivative, an integral, a differential equation, or its solution—can be expressed in terms of a very small repertoire of primitive concepts. In a type‑theoretic foundation of mathematics there are essentially only two basic types, *e* (entity) and *t* (Boolean truth), and all other types, notions, and concepts are built from these two. Hence mathematical reasoning is systematic: we know the full content of each concept. Occasionally we invent new concepts (the “poetics of mathematics”), but even then we can translate them, or suitable approximations, into existing concepts that trace back to the first principles. In this sense mathematical concepts are constructed, or at least describable, in a bottom‑up fashion. By contrast, reasoning about physics or the broader real world—ontology, metaphysics, nature, the social world, the humanities, emotions, mind, etc.—is far more difficult. We can only hypothesise what a concept eventually entails and how it relates to other concepts; we never possess a complete elucidation of its content. Every research programme uncovers new nuances, creates new concepts, merges old ones, and so on, all in a non‑rigorous manner because the underlying “first principles” are unknown. We do not even know which first principles would be appropriate for describing reality. The semantics of natural language provides a clear illustration of attempts to uncover such principles. For example, the table in *Elements of Formal Semantics* (Edinburgh University Press) shows how each grammatical category can be represented as a derived type built from the two basic types *e* and *t*. If mathematics is to serve as a model of the world, then the requisite first principles already exist; we merely need to express complex notions—such as “happiness according to Aristotle,” “ontology according to Hegel,” “ontology in a British encyclopedia,” or “ontology according to philosopher N.”—in terms of those basic mathematical notions. Of course, well‑defined concepts are rooted in the internal semantics of particular individuals, and only through collective conventions do they become the shared concepts of scientific communities, legal systems, etc. I recognise that my thoughts may sound naïve, which leads to my real question: Is there a discipline within philosophy that seeks to formulate the content of every concept using a small set of primitive notions or types (whether those are the familiar mathematical types or something else)? If so, what are the names of such philosophical fields? What are the common terms and research themes associated with them? I only need keywords and names; I can explore the details on my own.

title: Wittgenstein - self and ethics in the Tractatus
text: I think I have a fairly clear grasp of the relationship between ontology and the “logical syntax” of language as presented by Wittgenstein in the *Tractatus*. He posits the existence of atomic entities—mysterious, simple, unaltered objects about which he offers no examples (thesis 2.0211). For the sake of brevity I will refer to this class of objects as W‑objects. At the linguistic level, W‑objects correspond exclusively to names (thesis 3.221), and each is assigned a particular logical type (thesis 2.0123). Wittgenstein also speaks of *states of affairs*, i.e., configurations of W‑objects. In language these correspond to elementary propositions—configurations of names (thesis 3.21). Beyond these are propositions that are truth‑functions (in the sense of classical propositional calculus) of elementary propositions. This constitutes the pictorial theory of language. There are, of course, numerous subtleties in the Tractatus’s account of logical form and its ontological implications—issues that are especially intriguing to anyone trained in mathematical logic and formal ontologies. Here, however, I am concerned with the more mystical aspect of the work, which most readers find most puzzling. To motivate my question, note that Wittgenstein was influenced by Schopenhauer, who—following Kant—held that the will is a thing‑in‑itself. Traces of this influence appear in the solipsistic passages of the *Tractatus* (5.62–5.6331) and in thesis 6.43. Wittgenstein was also indebted to G. E. Moore, whose *Principia Ethica* argues that the good is a simple, unaltered entity. Yet in the *Tractatus* the good does not seem to be treated as a W‑object, despite thesis 6.4, which leaves the statement unexplained. *Edit:* By “A is an example of a W‑object” I mean roughly that there exists a propositional function f(x) with one free variable, belonging to the perfect language Wittgenstein describes, such that substituting A for x yields a legitimate sentence f(A); equivalently, A occurs as a name in some sentence of that perfect language. *Further edit:* In response to Conifold’s remarks on the relation between logical positivism and the *Tractatus*: twentieth‑century philosophy saw a vigorous debate between metaphysical and positivist readings of the work, each supported by serious arguments. Regardless of how that debate is resolved, my interest lies in the following question.
